rule: Evidence credits program models, not wording. A code or wording alone never earns more than "possible link, model not confirmed". Only claims an independent verifier fetched, with a verbatim excerpt, enter this file.

tiers.tested: Causal studies of a matching program model.
tiers.research-associated: Consistent correlational evidence (a meta-analysis, or several long-term studies that adjust for earlier achievement or attendance). Worded "is associated with"; earns no credit.
tiers.checked, not supported: The review looked and found no evidence strong enough.

programModels.name: School-day reading tutoring
programModels.description: Tutoring during the school day by trained, paid tutors (teachers, paraprofessionals or national service members such as AmeriCorps), at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, using a structured reading curriculum, in kindergarten to grade 3. Volunteer and virtual tutoring count only at the lower sizes below. Homework help or general after-school time does not qualify.
programModels.typicalEffect: SPARK (Milwaukee) randomized trial: 0.12 standard deviations on a national reading test. A one-year follow-on trial of the same model: significant gains on two reading tests. Education Corps randomized trial: 0.17 at mid-year. Push-in kindergarten tutoring: oral reading 0.23, district reading level 0.11. Paraeducator tutoring in grade 1: better on 5 of 6 tests. Reading Corps: significant gains in kindergarten to grade 3. Recovery-era study: one tutoring program 0.22 and small-group reading 0.33 on state tests. Nashville at scale: 0.04 to 0.09. Volunteer tutoring meta-analysis: 0.23. Virtual tutoring: 0.05 to 0.08 (one-to-one 0.07 to 0.12). Meta-analysis of small-group instruction by adults: about 0.35 to 0.45 on mixed measures. Plan on 0.05 to 0.15 on the state test.

programModels.name: School-day math tutoring
programModels.description: Tutoring by trained, paid tutors (teachers, paraprofessionals or national service members such as Math Corps), during the school day, at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, using a structured math curriculum. Volunteer tutoring and tutoring offered only before or after school do not qualify.
programModels.typicalEffect: Math Corps randomized trials: 0.17 (0.24 at intended dosage) and about 0.18 on broad math tests; the state test was not significantly different in the grades 4 to 8 and statewide trials. A matched study of another tutoring corps: 0.10. Early-grade protocols: Number Rockets 0.34, Pirate Math 0.37, fractions tutoring 0.51, small-group early math 0.19 (researcher or national tests). Tutoring meta-analysis 0.36. Recovery-era study: one tutoring program 0.22 on state math. Nashville at scale: no average math effect. Volunteer tutoring: math not significant. Plan on 0 to 0.10 on the state test.

programModels.name: Daily high school math tutoring with two students per tutor
programModels.description: Daily, in-school small-group math tutoring for ninth and tenth graders (Saga model, including the technology-blended version in which two students work with the tutor while two use software).
programModels.typicalEffect: Average 0.14 (three trials: 0.09, 0.14, 0.19); technology-blended version 0.23 for participants at about 30 percent lower cost. Meta-analysis: small-group instruction 0.38, math tests 0.34.

programModels.name: Structured social and emotional learning curriculum taught to whole classes
programModels.description: A universal, sequenced social and emotional learning curriculum taught to whole classes during the school day by trained teachers or partner staff, for at least a full school year. After-school or pull-out social skills groups and one-off assemblies do not qualify.
programModels.typicalEffect: Meta-analysis of school-based programs: overall 0.08 standard deviations (math 0.08, English 0.07), smaller in randomized trials than in quasi-experiments. Another meta-analysis: reading 0.25 and math 0.26, with smaller effects in large rigorous randomized trials. Positive Action in Chicago: the authors report a marginal math gain, the clearinghouse finds state reading and math not significant, and absenteeism improved. Positive Action in Hawaii: large gains per the authors, not significant in the clearinghouse review. INSIGHTS: early gains faded by middle school. A classroom social skills program: no main effects. Plan on 0.05 to 0.08 on state tests.

programModels.name: Personalized messages to families about their own child's absences
programModels.description: Repeated, personalized messages naming the child's own absences or missed learning, drawn from school records under a data-sharing agreement. A single letter at the 90-percent line, a standard legalistic truancy notice or general family events do not qualify.
programModels.typicalEffect: Texting trial in 4 urban districts (26,843 students, kindergarten to grade 5): chronic absence 2.4 to 3.6 percentage points lower from 20.5 percent (12 to 18 percent), 3.5 to 7.3 points lower for students with high prior absence, at about 6 to 9 dollars per student. 47 rural districts in 16 states: absences down 1.7 percent for the offer (about 0.2 days) and 4.5 percent for families reached (about half a day), at 4.07 dollars per student. Teacher postcards, preschool to grade 2: absences down 8.3 percent. Teacher-parent outreach in grades 1-2 in five schools: 5 to 6 points fewer students with 4 or more absences. Redesigned truancy notices: 0.07 fewer days absent than the standard notice.

programModels.name: Lead agency of a whole-school community school
programModels.description: The partner is the lead agency or full-time coordinator of a whole-school community school, with on-site health, family and learning services, sustained at least three years.
programModels.typicalEffect: New York City: chronic absence down 7.4 percentage points (elementary and middle) and 8.3 (high school), three-year average. California (matched schools, first full year): chronic absence fell 1.5 points more than in matched schools (about 30 percent more), 2.8 points in elementary schools. Tennessee (statewide, staggered adoption): chronic absence rose 1.3 points (5.9 percent). Plan on the California size, not the New York City size.

programModels.name: Paid summer job placement for high school students
programModels.description: A paid summer jobs program for high school students, filled by lottery or similar open selection, as in Boston.
programModels.typicalEffect: Boston lottery: higher on-time graduation and lower dropout (existing link). Chicago lottery: no significant change in school persistence through the third year after the program, with confidence intervals ruling out more than 4 to 5 more days present.

programModels.name: Ninth grade on-track monitoring from school records
programModels.description: A program serving ninth graders that tracks its own students' course passing and credits from school records (for example through a data-sharing agreement) and acts on them.
programModels.typicalEffect: Philadelphia: 82 percent graduation on track against 56 percent off track (87.8 to 89.2 against 43.3 to 48.8 percent in district cohorts); Chicago: on-track students 3.5 times more likely to graduate.

pathways.summary: Tutoring programs that build children's reading skills raise scores on standardized reading tests, and partner-run versions using trained, paid tutors (including national service members) work too, though effects are smaller at scale.
pathways.programModel: Tutoring during the school day by trained, paid tutors (teachers, paraprofessionals or national service members such as AmeriCorps), at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, using a structured reading curriculum, in kindergarten to grade 3. Volunteer and virtual tutoring count only at the lower sizes below. Homework help or general after-school time does not qualify.
pathways.typicalEffect: SPARK (Milwaukee) randomized trial: 0.12 standard deviations on a national reading test. A one-year follow-on trial of the same model: significant gains on two reading tests. Education Corps randomized trial: 0.17 at mid-year. Push-in kindergarten tutoring: oral reading 0.23, district reading level 0.11. Paraeducator tutoring in grade 1: better on 5 of 6 tests. Reading Corps: significant gains in kindergarten to grade 3. Recovery-era study: one tutoring program 0.22 and small-group reading 0.33 on state tests. Nashville at scale: 0.04 to 0.09. Volunteer tutoring meta-analysis: 0.23. Virtual tutoring: 0.05 to 0.08 (one-to-one 0.07 to 0.12). Meta-analysis of small-group instruction by adults: about 0.35 to 0.45 on mixed measures. Plan on 0.05 to 0.15 on the state test.
pathways.caveats: Most effects are on national or researcher tests, not the Pennsylvania test. Philadelphia's Experience Corps volunteer program (2016-17 only) showed no overall difference in kindergarten to grade 3, and the grade 3 comparison group scored slightly higher. Effects shrink as programs scale.

pathways.summary: Tutoring programs that build children's math skills raise scores on math tests, but at scale the gain on state tests is small or not detectable.
pathways.programModel: Tutoring by trained, paid tutors (teachers, paraprofessionals or national service members such as Math Corps), during the school day, at least three sessions a week, one-to-one or small groups, using a structured math curriculum. Volunteer tutoring and tutoring offered only before or after school do not qualify.
pathways.typicalEffect: Math Corps randomized trials: 0.17 (0.24 at intended dosage) and about 0.18 on broad math tests; the state test was not significantly different in the grades 4 to 8 and statewide trials. A matched study of another tutoring corps: 0.10. Early-grade protocols: Number Rockets 0.34, Pirate Math 0.37, fractions tutoring 0.51, small-group early math 0.19 (researcher or national tests). Tutoring meta-analysis 0.36. Recovery-era study: one tutoring program 0.22 on state math. Nashville at scale: no average math effect. Volunteer tutoring: math not significant. Plan on 0 to 0.10 on the state test.
pathways.caveats: Most gains are on non-state tests; the two Math Corps trials that used the state test found no significant difference.

pathways.summary: Daily small-group math tutoring in ninth and tenth grade raises high school math test scores.
pathways.programModel: Daily, in-school small-group math tutoring for ninth and tenth graders (Saga model, including the technology-blended version in which two students work with the tutor while two use software).
pathways.typicalEffect: Average 0.14 (three trials: 0.09, 0.14, 0.19); technology-blended version 0.23 for participants at about 30 percent lower cost. Meta-analysis: small-group instruction 0.38, math tests 0.34.
pathways.caveats: Outcomes are district or national tests, not the Keystone exam. Population was mostly entering ninth graders.

pathways.summary: Daily math tutoring cuts math course failures, and passing ninth-grade courses strongly predicts graduating in four years in Philadelphia and Chicago.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: not used for credit. Tested model: the Saga daily school-day tutoring model (see L-03).
pathways.typicalEffect: On-time graduation +1.9 percentage points for participants (standard error 3.4) against a 77.2 percent control mean, not significant; the range runs from a 4.8-point decline to an 8.6-point gain.
pathways.caveats: Correction: the draft said graduation was not measured. The same paper estimated on-time graduation directly: +1.9 points (standard error 3.4), not significant (Guryan and others 2021, working paper 21-12, pages 6 and 22, fetched by the methods reviewer at https://www.ipr.northwestern.edu/documents/working-papers/2021/wp-21-12.pdf). Non-math failures fell only in the first trial. The attendance gain in the researcher's note was contradicted by the checker.

pathways.summary: Daily math tutoring did not change total days absent in the larger Chicago trial; in the District of Columbia, students were less likely to be absent on the days they had tutoring.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Chicago first trial: plus 1.58 days absent (standard error 1.87), not significant. Earlier Chicago pilot of tutoring plus Becoming a Man (106 boys, one school): 10.3 fewer days absent for the offer, not significant after adjusting for multiple outcomes. District of Columbia tutoring initiative: 1.2 percentage points less likely to be absent on scheduled tutoring days (7 percent).
pathways.caveats: The District of Columbia estimate compares tutoring days with other days for the same students; no total or annual attendance effect was estimated, so it does not show a change in the 90-percent share. The Chicago pilot combined tutoring with a behavioral program.

pathways.summary: Classroom-based summer reading programs for low-income children modestly raise reading comprehension.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: classroom summer reading instruction for low-income children, focused on comprehension.
pathways.typicalEffect: Overall gain of 0.10 standard deviations on total reading; 0.20 on reading comprehension for mostly low-income samples; about zero for mixed-income samples.
pathways.caveats: The checker did not confirm that all included studies were randomized. Gains were limited to low-income samples. The national summer learning trial's randomized effect faded (its own row). Bounded by L-07: the national summer learning trial's randomized effect was gone by the spring state test.

pathways.summary: Voluntary summer learning programs gave small, short-lived gains; randomized trials found little effect on reading and no lasting state test advantage.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: National Summer Learning Project: reading 0.01, math 0.07 (not significant). Teach Baltimore: no average effect; students who attended two or more summers gained. Building Educated Leaders for Life summer program: about 0.08 in reading. Multi-summer middle school program: English up 0.06 once, no math gain. Meta-analysis: average 0.10 on mixed tests. Summer math at home: no effect. Philadelphia summer program: attendees scored slightly lower on the district's own test.
pathways.caveats: The multi-summer attendance gain is its own attendance link.

pathways.summary: Out-of-school-time programs with academic instruction raise achievement a little at best; experimental reviews find mostly null effects.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Review of experimental after-school evaluations: 84 percent of 97 impacts not significant. A meta-analysis found that including lower-quality studies changes conclusions. One program: moderate positive effect (size unknown).
pathways.caveats: Both meta-analyses mix randomized and comparison-group studies. The certified-teacher and traditional-instruction conditions were tested one at a time, not together. All effects were below 0.25 standard deviations. The researcher's note of harm for students with behavior problems was not confirmed. Bounded by the 21st Century Community Learning Centers null and the structured after-school reading result.

pathways.summary: A structured after-school math curriculum did not raise scores reliably.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: A tutoring software trial after school: not significant.
pathways.caveats: The comparison group also received teacher-led after-school math.

pathways.summary: Structured after-school reading instruction did not raise reading scores in randomized trials; one positive trial of a structured curriculum used non-state tests.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: A recent randomized trial: no significant differences, with high attrition and absence. A multi-year after-school academic program: second-year test effects positive but not significant (grade point average 2.58 versus 2.43). A structured after-school reading curriculum: vocabulary 0.23 and comprehension 0.32 on a national test, no effect on spelling or fluency.
pathways.caveats: The positive trial's location and test came from secondary sources.

pathways.summary: An intensive multi-year after-school academic program did not raise state test scores in its randomized trial, though grades rose.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No significant test impact in years 1 or 2; grade point average up by year 2.
pathways.caveats: Reading did not improve in the same trial. The test was a national standardized test. Washington, DC and Alexandria, Virginia. The researcher's 'later expansion study' was not confirmed.

pathways.summary: General after-school centers, including 21st Century Community Learning Centers, did not raise state test scores in the national randomized trial, and statewide matched comparisons find effects near zero, sometimes negative at low participation.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Covers 21st Century Community Learning Centers at any participation level. A program's own improvement percentages do not show an effect.
pathways.typicalEffect: Texas statewide: median center effect minus 0.02 standard deviations in math and reading; math minus 0.03 to minus 0.17 for students below 45 days and plus 0.03 at 120 or more days in two years; reading effects consistently negative. New Jersey 2019: English mostly null; math gains in grades 4 and 8; high versus low attenders plus 0.04 in math. New Jersey 2024: no significant test effects. Rhode Island: reading 0.055 at 30 or more days, math not significant. Washington: reading 0.03 and math 0.04 in one year, about zero the next. West Virginia: no differences. Philadelphia matched comparison: no state test difference. Recovery-era study: after-school and other added-time programs null.
pathways.caveats: Positive Louisiana and Indiana findings have no confirmed size, and Indiana's gain was only in math for students who failed in the fall. A study of high-quality programs found large gains, but against routinely unsupervised children and with change scores. Pennsylvania's state report percentages have no comparison group.

pathways.summary: Universal social and emotional learning curricula taught during the school day raise students' test scores slightly, and the gain is smaller in the largest, most rigorous trials than in earlier reviews.
pathways.programModel: A universal, sequenced social and emotional learning curriculum taught to whole classes during the school day by trained teachers or partner staff, for at least a full school year. After-school or pull-out social skills groups and one-off assemblies do not qualify.
pathways.typicalEffect: Meta-analysis of school-based programs: overall 0.08 standard deviations (math 0.08, English 0.07), smaller in randomized trials than in quasi-experiments. Another meta-analysis: reading 0.25 and math 0.26, with smaller effects in large rigorous randomized trials. Positive Action in Chicago: the authors report a marginal math gain, the clearinghouse finds state reading and math not significant, and absenteeism improved. Positive Action in Hawaii: large gains per the authors, not significant in the clearinghouse review. INSIGHTS: early gains faded by middle school. A classroom social skills program: no main effects. Plan on 0.05 to 0.08 on state tests.
pathways.caveats: The federal seven-program social and emotional learning trial could not use test scores (it used rating scales), so it neither supports nor refutes this link. A science effect (0.06) rests on three estimates and is not added. Program developers ran several of the positive trials.

pathways.summary: Two randomized trials of early social and emotional learning programs that followed children to graduation found no direct effect.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: INSIGHTS into Children's Temperament: on-time diploma 37.4 versus 37.1 percent. A Pennsylvania preschool program (Research-based Developmentally Informed Head Start): no direct effect on on-time graduation, with indirect effects through earlier gains.
pathways.caveats: The preschool trial had graduation data for 69 percent of the sample.

pathways.summary: Cognitive behavioral group sessions that teach adolescent boys to slow down automatic reactions raised graduation in the first trial.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: the Becoming a Man cognitive behavioral group curriculum for adolescent boys, with trained counselors, in school.
pathways.typicalEffect: Graduation up 6 to 9 percentage points (12 to 19 percent), first trial only; arrests down 28 to 35 percent during the program.
pathways.caveats: Graduation was measured in the first trial only. The two later trials found no significant effect on student outcomes (own row); across four trials school engagement rose 0.03 to 0.08 standard deviations. Boys only, Chicago. Dropout counts were not measured separately. Researchers also mapped this program to mental health, violence and justice codes (Y8.6, Y8.12, Y8.13). Merged reading: one trial raised graduation; two later trials at new sites found no effect on student outcomes (L-16).

pathways.summary: The same cognitive behavioral program at new sites showed no significant effect on student outcomes.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No statistically significant effect on student outcomes in the two later trials.
pathways.caveats: Program summary page, not a paper. Bounds the Becoming a Man graduation row.

pathways.summary: Brief classroom exercises that frame worries about belonging as normal at the start of middle school cut absences.
pathways.programModel: Two brief, scripted classroom writing exercises at the start of middle school that frame worries about belonging as normal and temporary, delivered to whole sixth-grade classes. We expect this to be rare among partners.
pathways.typicalEffect: 12 percent fewer absences than the control group, plus 18 percent fewer D and F grades and 34 percent fewer behavior referrals; cost about 1.35 dollars per student.
pathways.caveats: A preregistered randomized replication in three Texas schools (604 sixth graders) found no significant effect on attendance or any academic or behavioral outcome. One district-wide trial (11 middle schools in a Midwestern district). The absence figure is a relative change, not attendance-rate points.

pathways.summary: A belonging exercise cut discipline citations for Black boys through high school, and early misbehavior is one of the flags that predict not graduating in Philadelphia.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Discipline citations down 65 percent among Black boys (confidence interval 15 to 85 percent); no graduation estimate.
pathways.caveats: Only the second experiment (137 sixth graders) tested the belonging exercise alone. Discipline is not a SPOTlight indicator. The behavior flag is not a well-replicated stand-alone predictor in the checked sources.

pathways.summary: High schools that raise students' social well-being and effort raise graduation, beyond their effects on test scores.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Per standard deviation of school effect: graduation up about 1.5 percentage points (social well-being) and 1.6 (effort).
pathways.caveats: School value-added models (observational), not programs. Chicago ninth graders. Self-reported measures.

pathways.summary: Teachers who improve students' attendance, behavior and grades raise later outcomes such as finishing high school, beyond their test-score effects.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Adding non-test measures more than doubles the predictable variation in teacher effects on longer-run outcomes.
pathways.caveats: Teacher effects in North Carolina ninth grade, not a program.

pathways.summary: Writing about personal values, meant to ease stereotype threat, did not raise academic performance in a large replication.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No detectable effect; the estimates rule out benefits larger than 0.10 standard deviations.
pathways.caveats: Outcome was grades and related measures, not state tests.

pathways.summary: School-based mentoring did not raise test scores.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: National school-based mentoring trial: no significant impacts after correction (math proficiency odds ratio 0.94). Check and Connect in Chicago: no effect on test scores or grades. Meta-analysis of school-based mentoring: very small effects, largest 0.09 on self-esteem.
pathways.caveats: No academic-specific or test-score effect was retrieved from the meta-analyses. Larger effects for youth with existing difficulties.

pathways.summary: Check and Connect kept students with disabilities in school in earlier trials, but a later randomized trial in general education found no effect, so the dropout claim does not extend to general student populations.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Earlier positive trials were with students with disabilities; partners serving general populations cannot rely on them.
pathways.typicalEffect: A later randomized trial of Check and Connect with 553 students found no statistically significant impact on any measure.
pathways.caveats: The populations and designs of the earlier positive trials were not re-checked in this review.

pathways.summary: The monitoring and mentoring program Check and Connect showed no discernible effect on completing school, and a later randomized trial in general education also found no effect.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: A later randomized trial of Check and Connect with 553 students found no statistically significant impact on any measure.
pathways.caveats: Confirmed from the author abstract; the district-records data source and the site were not separately checked.

pathways.summary: Trained mentors who check in with chronically absent students added school days and kept more high school students enrolled.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: About 9 more days a year per previously chronically absent mentored student; mentored high school students 52 percent more likely to remain in school the next year.
pathways.caveats: Comparison of 100 pilot schools with 46 comparison schools; selection into mentoring is not addressed. New York City. Promising; would move up with a randomized or stronger comparison design.

pathways.summary: Warm teacher-student relationships go with more engagement, which partly carries a small link to achievement.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Medium to large associations with engagement and small to medium with achievement (no correlation values in the fetched abstract).
pathways.caveats: Correlational; teachers, not program staff.

pathways.summary: Students attending more school days is exactly what this indicator counts. This is a definition, not evidence that any program type moves attendance.
pathways.programModel: Any program, provided the partner shows from school records that its participants' share at or above 90 percent of days rose against a comparison group. A program model with a tested attendance effect (L-28, L-36) gives a reason to expect it; other models need their own data.
pathways.typicalEffect: Not applicable: the size depends on the program. Program models with tested attendance effects are in L-28 (messages to families) and L-36 (community schools).
pathways.caveats: The trial figures in the draft belong to L-28 and were removed here. Chronic absence (missing 10 percent or more of days) is close to the complement of this indicator, but District enrollment rules can differ. School asthma education (L-66), school health centers (L-65) and tutoring (L-05) did not move school-record attendance, so a program type alone is no reason to expect a gain.

pathways.summary: Personalized messages to families about their own child's absences (mailings, texts or teacher-written postcards) correct parents' underestimates, and their children then miss fewer days.
pathways.programModel: Repeated, personalized messages naming the child's own absences or missed learning, drawn from school records under a data-sharing agreement. A single letter at the 90-percent line, a standard legalistic truancy notice or general family events do not qualify.
pathways.typicalEffect: Texting trial in 4 urban districts (26,843 students, kindergarten to grade 5): chronic absence 2.4 to 3.6 percentage points lower from 20.5 percent (12 to 18 percent), 3.5 to 7.3 points lower for students with high prior absence, at about 6 to 9 dollars per student. 47 rural districts in 16 states: absences down 1.7 percent for the offer (about 0.2 days) and 4.5 percent for families reached (about half a day), at 4.07 dollars per student. Teacher postcards, preschool to grade 2: absences down 8.3 percent. Teacher-parent outreach in grades 1-2 in five schools: 5 to 6 points fewer students with 4 or more absences. Redesigned truancy notices: 0.07 fewer days absent than the standard notice.
pathways.caveats: Effects are small per student and smaller at scale. A single nudge letter at the 90-percent line had no overall effect (a middle school subgroup improved). Texts about grades and attendance in grades 6-11 in one Midwest district did not change chronic absence. Partners need record access through the school or district.

pathways.summary: Frequent messages to parents about missed work, grades and absences kept more students enrolled.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: weekly teacher-to-parent messages or automated texts about missed assignments, grades and absences.
pathways.typicalEffect: Share failing to earn course credit fell from 15.8 to 9.3 percent, mainly by preventing dropout (summer credit recovery); retention rose with weekly texts.
pathways.caveats: Short-run staying enrolled, not the annual dropout count. One trial was a summer credit-recovery program; the other was in Kanawha County, West Virginia.

pathways.summary: Frequent messages to parents cut course failures, and passing ninth-grade courses predicts four-year graduation in Philadelphia.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: weekly teacher-to-parent messages or automated texts about missed assignments, grades and absences.
pathways.typicalEffect: Course failures down 27 percent; on-track Philadelphia ninth graders graduated at 82 percent against 56 percent off track.
pathways.caveats: Graduation was not measured in the trials. Staying enrolled is not the same as graduating.

pathways.summary: Information to parents about their child's schoolwork raised grades, but effects on test scores were very small or absent.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. The attendance effect is covered by the family messaging link.
pathways.typicalEffect: Texts to parents about missed work in one district: grade point average up; math and reading tests not significant. England, texts to parents about tests and homework: math 0.067 and English 0.033 standard deviations, absenteeism down 0.054, science not significant.
pathways.caveats: The England English result may be biased (authors' note).

pathways.summary: Relationship-building teacher home visits were followed by slightly higher attendance and math scores in a matched study in the District of Columbia, but a St. Louis randomized trial found no differences.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: District of Columbia, grades 1-5 (matched comparison): attendance 95.28 against 94.93 percent (effect size 0.07); grades 4-5 math 0.11 standard deviations higher on combined state tests; reading not significant. St. Louis (teachers randomized within 11 schools): chronic absence 0.3 points lower, not significant; no academic differences. Connecticut's Learner Engagement and Attendance Program: attendance about 4 points higher in the month after a first visit for chronically absent students.
pathways.caveats: Families who accept visits differ from those who do not. The Connecticut study compares students visited earlier with students visited later, without matching on prior attendance, and its visits re-engaged chronically absent students, a different model. A Washoe County evaluation found no relationship once prior-year risk was controlled. The St. Louis trial had fidelity problems.

pathways.summary: A multifamily group program in Philadelphia kindergartens did not change parents' social support or children's academic learning.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No significant effects on any key outcome in the randomized trial, including parental social support and academic learning.
pathways.caveats: Among families attending 3 or more sessions (non-randomized), reading was higher at the end of grade 1 but kindergarten attendance was lower. The social-capital gain in the researcher's note came from a different trial in San Antonio and Phoenix.

pathways.summary: Parental involvement, especially high expectations, goes with higher achievement, and parental involvement programs go with gains.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: About 0.5 to 0.55 standard deviations across academic measures (2007 meta-analysis, urban secondary students); about 0.3 standard deviations for programs (2012).
pathways.caveats: The studies are largely associations; the randomized share was not established. Bounded by the Philadelphia family-program null.

pathways.summary: Mothers' education raised young children's school readiness, but no checked study links readiness to the grade 3 state test.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Eight months of maternal education: school readiness up 0.21 standard deviations.
pathways.caveats: The treatment was any education activity, not adult basic education alone. Only one corpus statement.

pathways.summary: Community schools that coordinate health, family and learning services on site cut chronic absence in New York City and California, but not in Tennessee.
pathways.programModel: The partner is the lead agency or full-time coordinator of a whole-school community school, with on-site health, family and learning services, sustained at least three years.
pathways.typicalEffect: New York City: chronic absence down 7.4 percentage points (elementary and middle) and 8.3 (high school), three-year average. California (matched schools, first full year): chronic absence fell 1.5 points more than in matched schools (about 30 percent more), 2.8 points in elementary schools. Tennessee (statewide, staggered adoption): chronic absence rose 1.3 points (5.9 percent). Plan on the California size, not the New York City size.
pathways.caveats: The Tennessee estimate is less certain because of pre-existing trends. Massachusetts Wraparound Zones, a lighter model, showed no attendance effect. Case management in Kalamazoo elementary schools improved attendance (size not checked), unlike the national case-management trial of integrated student supports.

pathways.summary: Community schools raised credit accumulation and graduation compared with similar schools.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: a whole-school community school sustained for three years (see L-36).
pathways.typicalEffect: Graduation 4.9 percentage points higher than comparison schools over three years (7.2 in year 3); credit accumulation up in all three years.
pathways.caveats: The graduation figure comes from the New York City schools' own summary of the RAND study. Credit accumulation, which RAND did confirm, is a neighbor of graduation, not the indicator.

pathways.summary: Community schools raised math scores by the third year in New York City, but other evaluations found no math change.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: New York City community schools: better state assessment results, significant in year 3, with no change in attendance, retention or suspension in this study. Tennessee integrated student supports: small English gain, no math change, and chronic absence rose. Michigan Communities In Schools: attendance was the only outcome affected. Harlem Children's Zone: the community programs alone did not explain the school's gains.
pathways.caveats: Mixed findings across cities; the New York City math effect size was not found by the checker.

pathways.summary: Community schools did not significantly raise English language arts scores over three years.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Positive but not significant in all three years.
pathways.caveats: RAND reports non-significant positive estimates, not evidence of no effect.

pathways.summary: Elementary-school coordinators who link each child to tailored supports went with lower later high school dropout.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Dropout 9.2 percent against 16.6 percent (about half the odds).
pathways.caveats: Propensity-weighted comparison, developer-run, in Boston; City Connects students began with lower report-card scores. Middle school test gains come from program pages only; the grade point average claim was not confirmed. Promising; needs independent replication.

pathways.summary: Case management and early-warning school reform improved some intermediate outcomes, but large randomized studies found no overall effect on graduation.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: A large randomized study of a school-based support program (2,528 students) found small, non-significant effects on graduation overall, with notable variation by site and over time. A school-level comparison found that Communities In Schools schools had larger gains in on-time graduation and larger dropout reductions, more so with high-fidelity implementation.
pathways.caveats: The program in the large study is not named in the source the checker reached. The Communities In Schools result is school-level and non-randomized, and the randomized evidence outweighs it.

pathways.summary: Collective-impact networks have no measured causal effect on student outcomes.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No effect sizes; communities with the most infrastructure growth tended to see more indicators improve.
pathways.caveats: Commissioned evaluation; authors say the results are not definitive.

pathways.summary: After-school programs that use sequenced, active, focused and explicit practices show test gains in weak studies.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: High-quality programs versus unsupervised peers: large math change-score gains. New York City: some quality features went with higher scores, others lower. Quality-restricted meta-analysis: conclusions change.
pathways.caveats: The quality comparison is between studies, not tested within a study. Program quality appears as a condition on the social and emotional learning row instead.

pathways.summary: Regular participation in 21st Century Community Learning Centers after-school programs (30 or more days a year) is associated with slightly fewer school-day absences than matched non-participants with similar prior-year attendance. Randomized trials have not shown that the programs cause this.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Texas statewide: regular participants attended 0.3 to 1.4 percentage points more school days than matched non-participants (about 0.5 to 3.4 days a year, more at higher participation); two years at 60 or more days a year added about 1.1 to 1.2 points. New Jersey 2022-23: unexcused absence rate about 0.4 points lower (about three quarters of a day) than students who attended 15 days or fewer. Washington 2012-13: 14 percent (30 or more days) and 33 percent (60 or more days) fewer unexcused absences. Texas site-level study (779 centers): median center effect 0.14 standard deviations, with wide spread. Philadelphia (11 grantees): elementary regular participants were less likely to have 10 or more unexcused absences; no difference in middle or high school. Gains this size move the 90-percent share only for students close to the line.
pathways.caveats: Students who keep coming differ from those who do not, and matching on prior attendance handles this only in part. A meta-analysis of controlled studies of after-school programs for at-risk youth found a small, non-significant attendance effect, and randomized trials of middle school after-school programs and of After School Matters in Chicago found no attendance difference. Most state reports come from one evaluator (American Institutes for Research); the Texas site-level and Philadelphia studies are by other evaluators. New Jersey's 2022-23 comparison group is low-attending participants, not non-participants. Two arts-focused Philadelphia centers found no attendance difference. Test-score effects are near zero.

pathways.summary: Coaching that changes how adults teach raises students' achievement, but partners earn no credit unless they coach classroom teachers.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Philadelphia Ongoing Assessment Project: grade 4 state math 11 scale points higher in year 1, 7 (not significant) in year 2. A multi-year teacher program: math 0.05 to 0.09 and reading 0.06 by year 4, absence down slightly.
pathways.caveats: Tested with classroom teachers (mostly literacy coaching in pre-kindergarten and elementary), not out-of-school-time staff. The 0.20 figure for content-specific coaching was not verified.

pathways.summary: Tutoring by teachers and paraprofessionals produces larger gains than tutoring by volunteers or parents, which suggests that tutor skill matters.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Effects largest for teacher and paraprofessional tutors (pooled 0.29 standard deviations overall).
pathways.caveats: The tutor-type contrast is between studies, not a test of training. Use as a condition on the tutoring rows.

pathways.summary: Teacher attendance in the United States responds to district policy (performance standards, tenure rules, leave policies), and teacher absence lowers student achievement; no partner program has been tested.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. District staffing policy.
pathways.typicalEffect: 10 more days of teacher absence lowered grade 4 math by 0.032 (another study: 0.017 math, 0.009 reading). Performance standards cut teacher absences about 10 percent; Chicago's probationary rules cut them about 10 percent; extended tenure periods reduced absences. Substitutes cost about as much learning as a much weaker teacher.
pathways.caveats: Not United States; employer incentives, not partner programs; A1.3 is partner staff well-being, not district teachers.

pathways.summary: A girls' after-school science program went with more high science performance in the program's own data; the strongest out-of-school science study found only a very small grade 8 gain.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Museum partnership in New York City: about 0.05 standard deviations on the grade 8 science exam.
pathways.caveats: Program-run evaluation with self-selection; Texas test; no evidence for the Keystone Biology exam.

pathways.summary: School arts partnerships with teaching artists raised writing scores on a state test.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: full-year school-based arts partnerships with teaching artists.
pathways.typicalEffect: Writing up 0.13 standard deviations; reading, math and science unchanged.
pathways.caveats: Houston; only grades 4 and 7 take the Texas writing test; schools applied and principals committed. Reading did not change (own row), and the Pennsylvania English language arts test is mostly reading.

pathways.summary: Arts experiences and music training did not raise reading, math or science scores in the strongest studies.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Oregon arts integration randomized trial: no significant state test effects (minus 0.03 to 0.05). Another arts program: no English advantage in later cohorts; no math difference. National analyses: music students did not outperform once differences were controlled. Drama program: higher odds of passing English; music-math meta-analysis 0.36 (designs unknown).
pathways.caveats: Positive studies have weak or unknown designs.

pathways.summary: Arts partnerships cut disciplinary infractions, and early misbehavior is one of the flags that predict not graduating in Philadelphia.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Infractions down 3.6 percentage points; elementary school engagement up (no size).
pathways.caveats: Discipline is not a SPOTlight indicator. The press figure of 20.7 percent was not found.

pathways.summary: Arts course-taking went with a fraction of a day more attendance in Boston, but the Houston arts trial found no attendance effect.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Boston: attendance up 0.2 percent (about a third of a day a year), 1.1 days for previously chronically absent students; Houston: no significant effect.
pathways.caveats: Boston course-taking is during the school day; fixed-effects design, not randomized.

pathways.summary: Low-income students with many arts credits graduated more often than those with few.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Did not graduate: 22 percent of low-arts against 4 percent of high-arts low-income students.
pathways.caveats: Correlations only, one dataset, within low-income students.

pathways.summary: Arts-integration partnership schools in Chicago scored higher in reading and math at the elementary level.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Significant elementary effects in 52 comparisons; no effects at grade 8.
pathways.caveats: Non-random school selection; 1990s data.

pathways.summary: A single art museum visit raised critical thinking about art, but nothing links that to the state English language arts test.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Critical thinking up 0.09 standard deviations overall, about three weeks after the visit.
pathways.caveats: Researcher measures, short-term, Arkansas.

pathways.summary: Steady extracurricular involvement, especially athletics, goes with lower dropout among at-risk students.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Consistent involvement: odds ratio 0.32 for dropout; at-risk prior participants dropped out markedly less.
pathways.caveats: Observational; one United States and one Canadian sample; middle school arts was not related to dropout.

pathways.summary: Playing on a school sports team is associated with fewer absences during the season, comparing each student with themselves.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Indiana (about 262,000 high school students, student fixed effects): absence rate 0.70 points lower in season (0.89 for team sports). Earlier study (existing row): unexcused absences declined for male athletes, partly offset the day after games.
pathways.caveats: Within-student designs control fixed traits but not season-specific motivation. The Indiana chronic-absence gap (10 against 23 percent) is descriptive. Transfer to partner sports programs is untested.

pathways.summary: Athletes complete more schooling, but much of the gap reflects who chooses to play.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Not quantified in the abstract.
pathways.caveats: Selection; attainment, not on-time graduation.

pathways.summary: Physical activity programs may help math slightly, but trials disagree.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: After-school exercise trial: the clearinghouse study page lists math as not significant, while its earlier quick review reported about 0.30 for the high dose. A classroom physical activity trial: no significant academic effects (only 55 of the planned 100 minutes a week delivered).
pathways.caveats: Math benefits appeared for physical activity combined with academic instruction for 6 to 10 weeks. Mostly school-day physical education, not after-school sports.

pathways.summary: Physical activity programs showed a small reading gain in one meta-analysis and no academic effect in a larger meta-analysis of randomized trials.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Reading 0.13 standard deviations (26 studies); overall academic achievement 0.14, not significant (92 randomized trials).
pathways.caveats: Children aged 4 to 13; multiple countries.

pathways.summary: Coached recess cut bullying and sped the return to class but did not change attendance, discipline or proficiency.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No impacts on attendance, discipline or proficiency; transition time 6.8 against 10.3 minutes.
pathways.caveats: Teacher-reported climate gains; 29 low-income schools in six cities.

pathways.summary: Schools with coached recess showed a very small attendance gain.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Attendance up about 0.2 percent; 0.4 percent for previously chronically absent students (about two-thirds of a day a year).
pathways.caveats: Treatment schools were poorer than comparisons; the randomized trial found no attendance effect.

pathways.summary: Engagement is the theorized path from interest and participation to attendance and staying in school.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Not applicable (review).
pathways.caveats: Narrative review; framing only.

pathways.summary: School eye exams and free glasses gave a small one-year gain that faded.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Baltimore: about 2 percentage points higher on the reading and math tests with screening, exams and free glasses; the effect faded over time; screening alone was not enough.
pathways.caveats: Baltimore; a co-author consulted for the eyeglass supplier.

pathways.summary: Primary care at school-based health centers did not reduce dropout or raise graduation.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: School-based health centers: suspensions fell about 1.1 points (18 percent) but no effect on dropout. Another study: health center presence went with college preparation but not with graduation rates.
pathways.caveats: Both studies checked from abstracts.

pathways.summary: School asthma education did not change school-record absences.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No difference in school-record absences in two trials; parent-reported asthma absences down 34 percent in one.
pathways.caveats: Children with asthma only.

pathways.summary: Across many attendance interventions, average effects on attendance are small and vary widely by model.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit; a magnitude benchmark for checking logic models, not a model.
pathways.typicalEffect: 22 controlled United States studies to 2018: 0.25 standard deviations (range 0.14 to 0.36); the family-school partnership range includes zero. 13 United States studies from 2020 to 2025: 0.09. Meta-analysis of randomized trials (61 articles): parental engagement 0.43 more days (range 0.10 to 0.76). 49 United States school-based studies from 2016 to 2025 with school-record attendance: chronic absence minus 0.054 standard deviations overall, minus 0.107 for messages to parents, minus 0.073 for whole-school approaches. Indicated interventions for students already missing school: moderate positive effects with wide spread (pooled size not checked).
pathways.caveats: Pooled sizes mix models. The 49-study figures come from a summary, not the full report, and its categories are curriculum, mentoring, family connectedness, parent messaging and whole-school. A claimed attendance gain well above about 0.1 to 0.25 standard deviations should be questioned.

pathways.summary: A later school start time meant more sleep and fewer first-period absences at one disadvantaged school.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: 34 more minutes of sleep; fewer first-period tardies and absences at one of two schools.
pathways.caveats: District policy, not a program; pre-post comparison.

pathways.summary: Nearby homicides briefly lower children's test performance, but no checked study shows a program reducing that violence.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Reading about 0.66 standard deviations lower within 4 days of a nearby homicide, for African-American children.
pathways.caveats: Chicago; the effect fades within days.

pathways.summary: A Chicago summer jobs program cut violent-crime arrests but showed no gain in schooling.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Violent-crime arrests down 43 percent; no evidence of improved schooling outcomes.
pathways.caveats: The schooling null comes from a summary. Bounds the summer jobs rows.

pathways.summary: A paid summer job raised attendance the next school year, most for older students who had been missing school.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: paid summer jobs for high school students.
pathways.typicalEffect: About 1 percent higher attendance overall and 3 percent for higher-risk students (New York City); 27 percent less chronic absence (Boston working paper).
pathways.caveats: The 1 and 3 percent figures come from the authors' companion paper. The Chicago trial showed no schooling gain, and J-PAL says the New York City and Chicago programs did not seem to raise school engagement.

pathways.summary: Winning a summer jobs lottery in Boston raised on-time graduation and cut dropout; a Chicago summer jobs trial found no change in school persistence.
pathways.programModel: A paid summer jobs program for high school students, filled by lottery or similar open selection, as in Boston.
pathways.typicalEffect: Boston lottery: higher on-time graduation and lower dropout (existing link). Chicago lottery: no significant change in school persistence through the third year after the program, with confidence intervals ruling out more than 4 to 5 more days present.
pathways.caveats: One positive city trial and one null on persistence, so suggestive only. The older Summer Training and Education Program trial does not test summer jobs because its control group also had a summer job (dropout 29.2 versus 25.1 and 21.6 versus 22.6 percent, not significant). The dropout part is weaker than the graduation part.

pathways.summary: Summer jobs raised end-of-course exam passing slightly, mainly for repeat participants.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: 0.023 more exams passed; mean exam scores about 0.008 standard deviations (not significant); small or no effects for first-time participants.
pathways.caveats: New York Regents exams, not Keystone; subgroup effect.

pathways.summary: Attending a full-time technical high school raised on-time graduation in lottery studies.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. School enrollment, not a partner program.
pathways.typicalEffect: Philadelphia career and technical high schools, admission lottery: significantly better graduation, credit accumulation and math course completion. Baltimore career and technical admission offers: more students completed a career pathway, but grade point averages were lower.
pathways.caveats: Baltimore attendance and graduation estimates could not be checked. Other Philadelphia outcomes were inconsistent across cohorts.

pathways.summary: Admission to a career academy or technical high school reduced ninth-grade absences.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit: school enrollment, not a partner program.
pathways.typicalEffect: Wake County, North Carolina technology career academy (admission lottery): about 1.4 fewer ninth-grade absence days (38 percent of the control mean). Connecticut (existing row): attendance up 1.7 points for boys.
pathways.caveats: School model.

pathways.summary: Technical high schools showed higher test scores in some analyses but no clear effect at the admission cutoff.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Higher test scores for boys (Connecticut); no clear effect at the Massachusetts admission cutoff.
pathways.caveats: The Massachusetts low-income gain comes from regression with controls, not the cutoff design.

pathways.summary: Career academies raised later earnings but did not raise high school completion overall in the national trial; a later lottery study in one North Carolina district found higher graduation, mostly for boys.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Career academies are a school structure, not a partner program.
pathways.typicalEffect: Wake County, North Carolina, admission lottery: graduation and college enrollment each up about 8 percentage points (about 9 percent of the comparison rate), concentrated among boys, with fewer ninth-grade absences.
pathways.caveats: One district. The 1990s multi-site randomized trial found no completion effect, so the evidence is mixed.

pathways.summary: Early-college career high schools did not change four-year graduation.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No significant difference in four-year graduation; dual enrollment up 26 points; degree completion up 5 points.
pathways.caveats: New York City.

pathways.summary: Technical skills are what the industry certification exam measures; one Pennsylvania study found cooperative education students scored higher on it, but no study tested a partner program.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Pennsylvania: cooperative education participants scored significantly higher on the occupational competency exam. Pennsylvania technical skill scores went with postsecondary enrollment. North Carolina certification earners did not earn more within seven years. Programs of study: industry credential earning was low.
pathways.caveats: The cooperative education study's controls could not be read beyond the abstract.

pathways.summary: A college-preparation program did not raise high school graduation.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No effect on total credits, grades or high school graduation; about one in five took an extra math course.
pathways.caveats: Corrected citation: Upward Bound reports (Mathematica 2004), not GiveWell's Talent Search page.

pathways.summary: Passing ninth-grade courses and earning credits strongly predicts graduating in four years, including in Philadelphia. Credits are also a graduation requirement by rule.
pathways.programModel: A program serving ninth graders that tracks its own students' course passing and credits from school records (for example through a data-sharing agreement) and acts on them.
pathways.typicalEffect: Philadelphia: 82 percent graduation on track against 56 percent off track (87.8 to 89.2 against 43.3 to 48.8 percent in district cohorts); Chicago: on-track students 3.5 times more likely to graduate.
pathways.caveats: Predictive, not causal. No checked study shows that a program-caused rise in course passing raises graduation: the Saga tutoring trial cut course failures but its direct graduation estimate was not significant (L-04), and Diplomas Now moved warning flags without moving graduation (L-41).

pathways.summary: Missing school lowers on-time graduation.
pathways.programModel: Same as L-27: school-record attendance gains for the partner's own students, against a comparison group.
pathways.typicalEffect: 10 more ninth-grade absences lower the probability of on-time graduation by about 2 percent (California).
pathways.caveats: The causal estimate is from one California district and uses class absences.

pathways.summary: More days in school cause higher reading and math scores, most clearly in the middle grades.
pathways.programModel: A mechanism link: a partner earns credit through one of its own tested attendance links (for example personalized absence messages to families, or Check and Connect in grades 5 to 7), then this link sizes the test effect.
pathways.typicalEffect: California: 10 more absences lower English by 0.05 and math by 0.08 standard deviations, more in grades 6 to 8. Philadelphia: a likely causal negative effect of absences on reading and math. Chicago Longitudinal Study: chronic absence lowered grade 8 math by 0.17; reading not significant. Sizing check: the 0.5 to 3.4 extra days linked to 21st Century Community Learning Centers participation imply at most about 0.02 in math.
pathways.caveats: Effects are small per day; elementary effects are flatter.

pathways.summary: Changes to how or when school breakfast is served gave mixed attendance results: breakfast after the bell lowered chronic absence, while universal free breakfast and breakfast in the classroom did not change attendance.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit: school meal policy, and Philadelphia already provides universal free meals.
pathways.typicalEffect: Breakfast after the bell, Colorado and Nevada (regression discontinuity, 1,883 schools): chronic absence 8.9 against 16.9 percent (clearinghouse effect size 0.44). Federal universal free breakfast pilot (schools randomly assigned, six districts): no effect on attendance or tardiness. New York City breakfast in the classroom: no attendance effect. Philadelphia classroom breakfast trial (existing row): no attendance effect.
pathways.caveats: School meal policy, not partner programming.

pathways.summary: Universal free school meals raise test scores very slightly at most.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. School meal policy.
pathways.typicalEffect: South Carolina: about 0.06 in elementary math. Another state: math 0.03, reading 0.08. New York City: small and imprecise. Arkansas: little effect. Breakfast mandates: math 0.08 to 0.09. Universal breakfast pilot: no effect.
pathways.caveats: Philadelphia already has universal meals, so the high-poverty null applies.

pathways.summary: Housing subsidies and rapid rehousing for homeless families did not improve children's attendance, and rehousing families outside the city raised absences.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. If a partner rehouses families, keeping children in their school of origin with transport is the implied condition.
pathways.typicalEffect: Randomized assignment of 172 students in homeless families in one city: children assigned to usual care did as well as or better than those assigned to housing interventions on attendance, mobility and achievement. One large urban district (within-student comparison): rapid rehousing and prevention lowered behavior incidents but raised absence and chronic absence, most for students rehoused outside the city.
pathways.caveats: One city each. The randomized study's link to a national housing trial and its use of school records were not confirmed.

pathways.summary: Homelessness and eviction are associated with more school absences, and eviction itself causes more absences and school changes.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Los Angeles (weighting on grade 3 attendance and math): homeless students missed 5.8 more days. Chicago and New York City (random assignment of eviction cases to judges): eviction raised the share of days absent by 2.4 percentage points (about 4.3 days) and chronic absence by 8.8 points, and increased school changes.
pathways.caveats: Programs that rehoused families did not raise attendance. The eviction study found little effect on grade 3 to 8 test scores, so no link to the grade 3 reading test is claimed and S5 is dropped from this row.

pathways.summary: More family income raised young children's achievement in welfare experiments, but recent work on the Earned Income Tax Credit finds small or no effects.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: 1,000 dollars more a year: 0.05 to 0.06 in early grades. Recent instrumental-variable study rules out more than 0.03 per 1,000 dollars.
pathways.caveats: National survey sample; a household transfer, not a program; the correction lowered the estimates by 32 percent.

pathways.summary: Giving girls sanitary products did not change school attendance.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No effect on the small attendance gap during menstruation.
pathways.caveats: Nepal.

pathways.summary: A short growth-mindset lesson raised grades for lower achievers, but no checked study links that grade gain to graduation.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Core grade point average up 0.10 points among lower-achieving ninth graders.
pathways.caveats: Larger where peer norms support challenge.

pathways.summary: Academic self-concept (how capable students believe they are in school subjects) is associated with slightly higher later test scores, compared with students who started at the same achievement level.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: A small path of about 0.08 from self-concept to later achievement, net of earlier achievement, in both meta-analyses. The path from achievement to later self-concept is about twice as large (0.16).
pathways.caveats: Holds for academic self-concept, not for growth mindset or general self-esteem (Self-Worth, Y5.4), where national long-term studies found no association once earlier achievement is counted. For self-efficacy, a meta-analysis found that in children only earlier performance predicts later self-efficacy, not the reverse. A 2024 reanalysis argues that adjusting for an earlier score can produce spurious effects of this kind.

pathways.summary: Raising general self-esteem does not improve school performance.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Modest correlations only; no causal effect shown.
pathways.caveats: General self-esteem only.

pathways.summary: Academic behaviors shape course grades, according to a literature review.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: None (qualitative).
pathways.caveats: No effect sizes.

pathways.summary: A philosophical inquiry program did not raise reading or math attainment.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No evidence of impact on reading or maths.
pathways.caveats: England; 198 schools.

pathways.summary: A statewide pre-kindergarten program left children behind on later state tests, and a Boston program showed no test effect.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Grade 6: English language arts minus 0.13, math minus 0.18 standard deviations (Tennessee); no detectable test effect (Boston).
pathways.caveats: District and state pre-kindergarten, not partner programs.

pathways.summary: Universal public pre-kindergarten in Boston raised high school graduation.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: full-day public pre-kindergarten of the Boston type.
pathways.typicalEffect: High school graduation up 6.0 percentage points.
pathways.caveats: No test-score effect; Tennessee pre-kindergarten harmed later test scores.

pathways.summary: Structured volunteer service with classroom discussion cut course failure in older studies, but none of those studies met clearinghouse standards.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: The clearinghouse found that none of seven in-scope studies of the Teen Outreach Program met its standards, so no conclusion is possible.
pathways.caveats: Four studies used outcomes not defined for dropouts and three lacked baseline equivalence.

pathways.summary: Civic engagement in young adulthood goes with more education later, but it happens after high school.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: this link is not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Positive associations; no sizes.
pathways.caveats: Ages 18 to 27; cannot affect four-year graduation.

pathways.summary: Out-of-school-time programs that follow the four recommended practices (sequenced, active, focused, explicit) showed achievement-test gains that other programs did not.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Tested model: after-school programs using sequenced, active, focused and explicit skill practice.
pathways.typicalEffect: 0.20 standard deviations on achievement tests for programs using the practices against 0.02 for others (10 studies each).
pathways.caveats: About a third of the included studies were randomized; the achievement estimate rests on 10 studies; the article's own text (0.31) and tables (0.20) disagree.

pathways.summary: Failing courses and low grades in the middle grades or ninth grade are associated with later dropping out, beyond what eighth-grade test scores and background predict.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: In Philadelphia, sixth graders who failed math were 54 percent less likely to graduate, and those who failed English 42 percent less likely. In Chicago, freshman grades and course failures explained about 39 percent of the variation in graduation, against about 12 percent for test scores and background.
pathways.caveats: These are early-warning predictions, not effects of raising grades. Most studies count students who did not graduate rather than the District's dropout count. The Philadelphia cohorts are from the 1990s and 2000s.

pathways.summary: Low attendance in the middle grades or ninth grade is associated with later dropping out, alongside other risk factors.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Chicago Longitudinal Study: chronic absence in grades 4 to 6 went with an 18-point lower chance of four-year graduation and an 11-point lower chance of any completion by age 21, adjusted for kindergarten and grade 3 achievement.
pathways.caveats: The exposure is grades 4 to 6 only.

pathways.summary: More absences are associated with lower grade 3 reading and math scores.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Philadelphia elementary students: a higher share of unexcused absences went with greater risk, particularly in math; excused absences were less harmful.
pathways.caveats: Same author as an existing source, so it adds little independence.

pathways.summary: Students graduating within four years of first entering ninth grade is exactly what this indicator counts. This is a definition, not evidence that any program type raises graduation.
pathways.programModel: Any program, provided the partner shows from school records that its own students graduated within four years at a higher rate than a comparison group. A program model with a tested graduation effect (paid summer jobs) gives a reason to expect it; other models need their own data.
pathways.typicalEffect: Not applicable: the size depends on the program. The program model with a tested graduation effect is paid summer jobs for high school students; attendance gains may also help a little.
pathways.caveats: Added 2026-10-18 after the review, on a lead from the extractor export thread: the attendance identity had a row and the graduation identity did not. The basis is the SPOTlight wording in Severin's 2026-10-18 paste, not a study. Reaching dropouts was not added: whether a student who re-enrolls leaves the District dropout count depends on District enrollment rules that were not checked. Monitoring and mentoring (Check and Connect) and case management did not raise completion in the checked trials.

pathways.summary: Attention, task persistence and impulse control at school entry are associated with higher later reading and math scores, beyond children's early academic skills.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Effects are small. Early math skills predicted later scores most, then reading, then attention. In a national study, kindergarten executive functions predicted grade 2 scores by about 0.05 to 0.12 of a standard deviation after earlier achievement.
pathways.caveats: Holds for young children only: in two middle-school studies, self-control did not predict changes in test scores once earlier scores were counted (it did predict report-card grades). Academic Perseverance (Y1.10) fits early task persistence; Emotion Regulation and Coping (Y4.2) fits only its impulse-control part. Social skills and prosocial behavior were not associated with later scores in the same studies.

pathways.summary: High schools where students report better relationships with teachers are associated with fewer students dropping out, after accounting for tenth-grade math scores and background.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: In one study, a school one standard deviation higher on student-teacher relations had about 86 percent lower odds of a student dropping out, but only in schools under 1,500 students. In the other, a better relationship climate went with lower dropout by senior year.
pathways.caveats: This is about a whole school's relationship climate, not one student's mentor or relationship. In the first study the association disappeared in schools over 1,500 students, which matters for large Philadelphia high schools. Both studies count dropping out by senior year, not the four-year graduation rate. A meta-analysis of unadjusted associations found only a non-significant trend for poor teacher relationships and dropout. The same studies found no association with test-score gains.

pathways.summary: Students who do their homework, take part and pay attention in class are associated with lower dropout, compared with students at the same achievement level.
pathways.programModel: Not applicable: a research-associated link is not about a tested program model and earns no credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: In the national sample, teacher-rated academic engagement (standardized coefficient about -0.27) and student-reported behavioral engagement (about -0.30) each predicted lower dropout by grade 12, with test achievement (about -0.20) in the same model.
pathways.caveats: Narrow: two studies. In the national sample, achievement was measured at the same time as engagement, not before it, and behavioral engagement includes skipping and lateness, which overlaps attendance.

pathways.summary: Offering or attending a general after-school program did not reliably raise school-day attendance in randomized trials or in a meta-analysis of controlled studies, so after-school programs should not claim to raise attendance.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Applies to general after-school programs, including 21st Century Community Learning Centers, After School Matters apprenticeships and middle school after-school programs.
pathways.typicalEffect: Meta-analysis of after-school programs for at-risk youth (24 studies, 16 attendance estimates): small and not significant (a companion abstract reports 0.04 standard deviations, range minus 0.02 to 0.10). Randomized trials: no treatment-control difference in attendance for middle school programs (447 students), and no difference in days absent from transcripts for After School Matters (535 Chicago high school students). Pennsylvania 2023-24 state report: 66 percent of 7,149 participants at or below 90 percent prior-year attendance improved, with no comparison group.
pathways.caveats: Program attendance in the trials was often low. The Pennsylvania figure, and the federal measure it uses, reflect regression to the mean and never count as evidence. A review of five experimental after-school evaluations found 84 percent of 97 impacts not significant; its attendance estimate was not confirmed. The small adjusted association in state evaluations is recorded as a research-associated link.

pathways.summary: Perfect-attendance awards did not raise later attendance, and awards given after the fact lowered it.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. A do-not-do entry for partner guidance and logic-model checks.
pathways.typicalEffect: Pre-registered randomized field experiment, 15,329 students in grades 6-12 in 14 California districts: after-the-fact awards raised absences by 0.06 days in the target month (8.3 percent more); announced awards had no effect while in place and raised absences by 0.067 days after they ended.
pathways.caveats: One trial; it does not test recognition of improvement or group incentives.

pathways.summary: A trained Check and Connect monitor who reviews each student's attendance records and follows up with the student and family cut absences for students in grades 5 to 7.
pathways.programModel: Check and Connect delivered with fidelity: a trained monitor assigned to each student, regular review of the student's attendance from school records, and structured follow-up with student and family, for students in grades 5 to 7. General mentoring does not qualify.
pathways.typicalEffect: Chicago randomized trial (grades 1 to 8): students who took part in grades 5 to 7 had 4.2 fewer absences a year (22.9 percent); no detectable effect in grades 1 to 4; no effect on test scores or grades.
