pathways.caveats: One trial, and the 4.2-day figure is the effect on students who took part, concentrated in one grade band. A Texas trial in middle and high schools, delivered by Communities In Schools and compared with its usual services, found no attendance effect, and a high school trial in a large urban district found no significant effects. The program cost about 1,700 dollars per participant a year.

pathways.summary: School-based, community, peer and college-access mentoring, and mentors or facilitators assigned to off-track students, did not reliably change school-record attendance, course passing or high school completion in randomized trials and matched studies.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Bounds Success Mentors and any mentoring logic model that claims attendance, on-track or graduation gains.
pathways.typicalEffect: Federal Student Mentoring Program trial (2,573 students, grades 4-8): absenteeism 5.03 against 5.49 percent (effect size minus 0.09), not significant after correction for multiple tests. Peer Group Connection: 161.2 against 161.6 days (grade 6) and 166.3 against 165.7 days (grade 9). College-access mentoring (FLIGHT, Florida): effect size 0.01 on days absent. Achievement Mentoring (393 students, grades 10-11): 1.7 more days attended and 0.67 more credits, neither significant; suspensions 20 against 30 percent. Mentoring of off-track students in five districts and a facilitator program at two urban high schools: no significant effects on attendance, course passing, promotion or completion. School-based mentoring meta-analysis: effects very small and mostly not significant. Meta-analysis of randomized attendance trials: mentoring 0.63 days, with a range that includes zero.
pathways.caveats: Exceptions are listed separately: Check and Connect in grades 5 to 7 and the education specialist for youth in foster care.

pathways.summary: A dedicated education specialist who meets regularly with youth in foster care and works across school and child-welfare systems raised their school attendance.
pathways.programModel: The Fostering Opportunities model: an education specialist for youth in foster care in grades 6 to 12, with weekly check-ins and liaison with child-welfare caseworkers.
pathways.typicalEffect: Colorado randomized trial (230 students in Jefferson County): attendance rate 7 percentage points higher at one year and 9 points at two years; clearinghouse effect size 0.49 (84 against 75 percent attendance in its 116-student sample).
pathways.caveats: One trial in one district; foster-care population only; the specialists were district staff in the trial.

pathways.summary: Weekly one-to-one play sessions with a trained paraprofessional for young children with low attendance and adjustment concerns were followed by higher attendance in one trial.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit until replicated. Model checked: Primary Project (screened kindergarten to grade 2 students, trained child associates, weekly playroom sessions).
pathways.typicalEffect: 249 students in seven schools of one northeastern city: attendance 87 against 84 percent (effect size 0.31); chronic absence 22 against 45 percent.
pathways.caveats: One compromised randomized trial (clearinghouse: meets standards with reservations); eligibility required both attendance below 90 percent and behavior concerns; developer-involved authors.

pathways.summary: One-to-one literacy tutoring during the school day combined with a family engagement worker raised early-grade school attendance as well as reading.
pathways.programModel: The SPARK (Future Forward) model as tested: paid tutors give kindergarten to grade 2 students one-to-one literacy sessions several times a week during the school day for at least a full school year, plus a family engagement worker who contacts and visits each family regularly. Tutoring alone or family engagement alone does not qualify.
pathways.typicalEffect: Milwaukee two-year trial (576 students, seven schools): absences effect size 0.20, significant (clearinghouse), with a literacy effect of about 0.23. Earlier Milwaukee cohort (496 students, six schools): about 3.3 fewer absences, effect size 0.18, not significant. One-semester trial in Alabama and rural Wisconsin (127 students): no attendance effect.
pathways.caveats: Developer-led evaluations; only one of three trials found a significant attendance effect, and the shortest found none. Effect sizes for the significant trial come from clearinghouse summaries.

pathways.summary: Summer programs that students return to over several summers, combining academics and enrichment, were followed by fewer school-year absences.
pathways.programModel: Multi-summer programs that students attend for two or more summers, combining academic and enrichment activities, with school-record attendance tracked (for example Horizons or Aim High). One-off camps do not qualify.
pathways.typicalEffect: Aim High, San Francisco: unexcused absence rate about 1.06 percentage points lower three years after first participation; students attending all three summers 58 percent less likely to be chronically absent in grade 8. Horizons (1,324 students, 15 sites): attendance 95.8 against 94.6 percent (effect size 0.15); elementary 1.1 points higher (about two days); chronic absence not significantly different.
pathways.caveats: Two quasi-experiments, no randomized trial; students who return for more summers may differ from those who do not. A school-break science camp in Knox County, Tennessee did not change attendance. Aim High funded its evaluation under an independence agreement. Test-score effects of summer programs are small.

pathways.summary: School-based telehealth clinics that let students be seen by a clinician during the school day cut absences and chronic absence.
pathways.programModel: The partner operates an on-site or telehealth clinic in the school that treats students during the school day. A nurse position alone, health education or health-system care coordination does not qualify.
pathways.typicalEffect: Three rural North Carolina districts (staggered openings): chronic absence down 2.5 percentage points (29 percent) and about 0.8 fewer days absent (10 percent). Six elementary schools with telehealth (4,203 students, adjusting for prior absences): 7.7 percent fewer absences (0.6 days a year).
pathways.caveats: No randomized trial; rural and small-city settings. A full-time licensed practical nurse in elementary schools gave negligible or slightly worse attendance; a health-system care-coordination trial for children with chronic conditions found no attendance difference; school asthma education was null. A Hawai'i high school nurse program lowered chronic absence two to three years after adoption (size not checked), but it is a different model.

pathways.summary: Online communities of practice for school licensed practical nurses focused on attendance lowered chronic absence in one trial; the version for registered nurses did not.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit until replicated.
pathways.typicalEffect: Cluster randomized trial in 84 urban elementary schools: significantly lower odds of chronic absence in schools whose licensed practical nurses joined (size not checked); no effect for registered nurses; about 764 to 896 dollars per school.
pathways.caveats: One district; the odds ratio was not checked; a partner's role would be facilitating district staff.

pathways.summary: Paid community members stationed along routes to school at arrival and dismissal (Safe Passage) lowered school absence rates.
pathways.programModel: A community organization hires, trains and deploys adults on designated routes to school at arrival and dismissal times, as in Chicago's Safe Passage.
pathways.typicalEffect: Chicago elementary schools (staggered rollout): absence rate down 0.58 percentage points (8.5 percent) in the published estimate; 0.78 points (11 percent) in the working paper. A separate study of the same program found violent crime down 14 percent and absenteeism down 2.5 points.
pathways.caveats: One city; school-level outcomes; both studies are quasi-experiments of the same program.

pathways.summary: Eligibility for a school bus or a full-fare transit pass raised attendance and cut chronic absence, while fare-free bus rides for students in one Florida county were followed by lower attendance.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit: transportation eligibility is a district or transit-agency decision. Partners that help families use passes or routes may cite it only as context.
pathways.typicalEffect: Michigan (walk-distance cutoffs, 50 largest districts): economically disadvantaged students' attendance up 0.5 to 1 percentage point and chronic absence down 2 to 4 points. New York City middle schools: a yellow bus or full-fare transit pass raised attendance 1.5 points (about 3 days). Leon County, Florida: fare-free rides for students went with lower attendance and more chronic absence.
pathways.caveats: The Florida study (synthetic control) was checked from its abstract only.

pathways.summary: Whole-school restorative practices reduced suspensions but did not reliably change attendance or chronic absence.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Pittsburgh school-randomized trial (44 schools): 0.92 fewer days absent (effect size minus 0.065) and 2 points less chronic absence, neither significant. Saint Paul (7 schools against 14 matched): no attendance improvement. Restorative practices added to Diplomas Now (33 schools randomized): fewer suspensions of 3 or more days; chronic absence reduction only marginally significant.
pathways.caveats: Suspension effects are real and belong to other pathways. A clearinghouse rated the Pittsburgh student-level attendance estimate promising (0.07), but it was not significant in the trial.

pathways.summary: Court-based truancy diversion did not improve attendance once regression to the mean was accounted for.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Also a methods warning: before-and-after gains for students chosen because of high absence are biased upward.
pathways.typicalEffect: Elementary students in five Minnesota districts (difference in differences against non-implementing schools): no program effect. Grades 7-10 in a Midwest county (matched against a neighboring county): similar or slightly lower attendance, no consistent pattern.
pathways.caveats: A community-based truancy court in a large urban district had fewer unexcused absences after one year than traditional court, but groups were matched on demographics only, and the city and baseline absences were not confirmed.

pathways.summary: A school early-warning and monitoring system cut chronic absence and course failure after one year in a United States trial, but a Norwegian trial found no effect on absence or completion, and no study measured graduation or dropout.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit: a school or district system. Partners who use school data to target students can describe it as a practice, not as an effect on these indicators.
pathways.typicalEffect: Midwest trial (73 high schools, 37,671 students): chronic absence 10 against 14 percent; course failure 21 against 26 percent; no effect on credits, low grade point average or suspension; dropout and graduation not examined. Norway (42 schools, 7,677 students): no significant effects on absence, completion or results after two years.
pathways.caveats: School-run; outcomes are one-year on-track steps.

pathways.summary: A school-wide social and character curriculum (Positive Action) was followed by lower school-level absenteeism in two cluster trials, but clearinghouse reviews of the same trials disagree on whether the effect is significant.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit until the conflict is resolved.
pathways.typicalEffect: Hawai'i (20 elementary schools): authors report 15.2 percent lower absenteeism; clearinghouse found it not significant (10.0 against 11.6). Chicago (14 schools): authors report lower absenteeism; one clearinghouse review found it not significant (5.6 against 7.0); another review of a paper from the same trial found a significant positive effect.
pathways.caveats: School-level outcomes; developer-involved trials.

pathways.summary: State human-services caseworkers placed in schools to help families with basic needs were followed by lower chronic absence.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit: Michigan's Pathways to Potential is run by the state human-services agency, and the evidence is one study without comparison schools.
pathways.typicalEffect: 160 Michigan schools (interrupted time series at staggered start dates): chronic absence about 8 percent lower (relative, not percentage points), about 21 students per school a year.
pathways.caveats: No comparison schools beyond staggered timing.

pathways.summary: Cash rewards to families tied to attendance, test scores and other activities did not raise attendance, test scores or graduation overall; welfare rules tying benefits to teen attendance raised some attendance measures but not completion.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Models checked: Opportunity New York City Family Rewards, Family Rewards 2.0 (Bronx and Memphis), Ohio's welfare initiative for teen parents, and a San Diego welfare attendance rule.
pathways.typicalEffect: Family Rewards (about 4,800 families): few effects for elementary and middle school students on attendance or tests; on-time graduation 49.2 against 48.2 percent overall; for ninth graders who were proficient readers, graduation up 8 points and 9.5 points more passed five or more Regents exams. Family Rewards 2.0: no effect on school progress through year 4 (on-time graduation 63.4 against 63.1). Ohio teen parents: high school or equivalency 34.0 against 31.9 percent, not significant. San Diego: more students met an 80 percent attendance rule; no difference in dropout or graduation.
pathways.caveats: Welfare sanctions are state policy, not partner programming.

pathways.summary: Longer exposure to whole-school inclusion programs (Special Olympics Unified Champion Schools) was followed by slightly lower absence for students with intellectual disabilities in grades 3 to 8 only.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: North Carolina (11 years, difference in differences): each year of exposure lowered the absence rate 0.3 points for students with intellectual disabilities in grades 3-8; in high school, a 0.01-point drop for other students and none for students with intellectual disabilities.
pathways.caveats: Schools chose their exposure; effects are small and limited to one group and level.

pathways.summary: Students who attend some multi-year after-school programs heavily and for several years drop out less and graduate on time more often than similar students, but the evidence comes mainly from one program and does not show the programs cause it.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Do not credit general after-school attendance, including 21st Century Community Learning Centers, with lower dropout or higher graduation.
pathways.typicalEffect: LA's BEST (Better Educated Students for Tomorrow) in Los Angeles: students who attended 168 or more days a year in grades 3 to 5 were 5 percent less likely to drop out and 6 percent more likely to graduate on time than matched students who never took part, with prior achievement and attendance adjusted; low attenders did worse than the comparison group. An earlier LA's BEST study: three or more years of participation went with lower dropout (size given only as test statistics); one year showed no difference. After School Matters in Chicago: students enrolled three or more semesters graduated more often (size and design not confirmed). A Boston middle school program: former participants were more than three times as likely to complete four years of high school (matching not confirmed).
pathways.caveats: Students who keep attending for years differ from those who stop. Both adjusted studies are of one program by one evaluation center, so they are not independent. Low attenders did worse, so the link depends on heavy, sustained participation. The California statewide 21st Century Community Learning Centers evaluation could not be reached by the checker.

pathways.summary: A school-based support program for ninth graders in one Philadelphia high school went with higher graduation but no change in school leaving.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Exito participants were 15 percentage points more likely to graduate; no significant difference in leaving school or in grade point average; attendance about 6 points higher in the second year only.
pathways.caveats: One school and one cohort. The comparison group came from earlier cohorts matched on demographics only, not on prior achievement. The null on leaving school sits awkwardly with the graduation gain.

pathways.summary: A multi-year out-of-school program for low-income middle and high school students raised credits and grade point average for lottery winners who started behind, which predicts but does not show higher graduation.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: StudentU in Durham, North Carolina, admission lottery: students with low baseline achievement gained 0.82 credits and 0.37 grade points and were 17.1 percentage points less likely to be suspended. Graduation was predicted to rise about 4 percentage points (5 percent) but was not observed.
pathways.caveats: Graduation itself was not measured. One program, one lottery study. The credit gains belong under the on-track link, not under graduation.

pathways.summary: Dropout prevention programs as a group reduce dropout in meta-analyses, but no single model a partner could run stands out, and effects shrink in the better-designed studies.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. A meta-analysis is not a model; credit needs a named model tested on dropout or graduation.
pathways.typicalEffect: Campbell review of dropout prevention programs: average odds ratio 1.72 (dropout from about 21 percent to about 13 percent); little variation by program type; larger with better implementation; smaller in studies with baseline equivalence. A later meta-analysis of 26 studies (2010 to 2022): average 0.19 standard deviations (range 0.10 to 0.28); behavioral programs 0.33, academic-only 0.12. A review of high school interventions: most research is on single-component programs for individuals or small groups.
pathways.caveats: Mixed designs and outcomes; the Campbell figures come from the review, not the interim abstract first cited. Y3.2 and Y1.13 dropped: the meta-analyses do not describe a mentoring or attendance model.

pathways.summary: Intensive multi-year mentoring, tutoring and stipends through high school (the Quantum Opportunity Program) raised graduation in a small pilot but not in a seven-site randomized replication.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. This is the closest graduation model a partner could run, and is worth revisiting if a newer trial appears.
pathways.typicalEffect: Seven-site randomized trial: no overall increase in diplomas; a short-run gain of 7 percentage points at the end of the program faded as the control group caught up, so participants got diplomas earlier, not more often. Five-site pilot: 63 percent of members graduated versus 42 percent of controls. A later Eisenhower Foundation trial: 76 versus 38 percent (300 students), checked only from the clearinghouse page.
pathways.caveats: The failed multi-site replication outweighs the positive pilot. Suggestive benefits for younger enrollees and some sites (including Philadelphia) are subgroup findings.

pathways.summary: A peer-led transition program for ninth graders went with higher graduation for boys in one school, but a later randomized trial found no effect on attendance, credits or promotion.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Peer Group Connection: boys graduated within four years at 81 versus 63 percent. Later North Carolina randomized trial: days attended 166.3 versus 165.7, credits 7.28 versus 7.27, promotion 88 versus 89 percent (all non-significant); suspensions 5 points lower.
pathways.caveats: The positive result is a subgroup in one school; whether the full sample improved was not confirmed. The replication was null on the steps that lead to graduation.

pathways.summary: Building Assets, Reducing Risks, a ninth-grade school model of teacher teams and relationship-building, cut course failure, but its effects on chronic absence and math were not consistent across trials and graduation was not measured.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. A school-run staffing model; partners cannot earn credit for it.
pathways.typicalEffect: Scale-up randomized trial: passed all core courses 80.2 versus 74.4 percent; chronic absence 19 versus 22 percent; college-readiness math test 0.07 standard deviations. Validation randomized trial: failed a core course 29.2 versus 40.6 percent; grade point average 2.58 versus 2.48; math test 0.01 (not significant); chronic absence not changed (23.1 versus 21.9 percent).
pathways.caveats: The journal article and the evaluation report of the validation trial differ on math. The math test was a national test, not the Keystone exam. Graduation was not an outcome in either trial.

pathways.summary: Students in career and technical programs of study, and students who earn industry certifications, graduate more often, but most of this evidence does not show adjustment for prior achievement.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: An instrumental-variable study of programs of study: enrollment raised the probability of graduating by 11.3 percent, with each added career and technical credit adding 4 percent; the causal graduation effect held in only one district. Certifications 'exert a meaningful influence' on graduation, more so for students at risk of dropping out (no size). Career and technical participation in one state went with higher graduation (no size).
pathways.caveats: Two of the three studies were checked from abstracts only, so their controls and sizes are unknown. Industry credential earning was low in the programs of study.

pathways.summary: School-to-career activities in high school went with lower dropout and higher graduation in one national survey analysis.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Participation in school-to-career activities reduced the probability of dropping out by about 5 to 6 percentage points; graduation was significantly higher, robust to test-score controls.
pathways.caveats: One survey-based study with no randomization; activities vary widely.

pathways.summary: Early college high schools raise graduation in lottery studies, but they are schools, not partner programs.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. A school model.
pathways.typicalEffect: National lottery study: 86 versus 81 percent graduated. North Carolina lottery study: five-year graduation up 3.1 percentage points.
pathways.caveats: Partners cannot earn credit for a school model.

pathways.summary: Career-focused high school programs with employer partners and paid internships did not raise school enrollment, graduation or credential earning in randomized trials.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Youth CareerConnect randomized trial: no significant effects on 20 survey outcomes (enrolled in high school 94.0 versus 92.8 percent; earned a credential 26.9 versus 28.9 percent); its matched comparison found attendance 0.7 percentage points higher (90.7 to 91.5 percent). Urban Alliance internships: graduated 98 versus 96 percent, not significant.
pathways.caveats: The Youth CareerConnect trial was underpowered. Graduation rates in the Urban Alliance sample were already near the ceiling.

pathways.summary: Advancement Via Individual Determination, a college-preparation elective, went with higher graduation in a matched study, but a schoolwide study found no change.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Students completing at least one elective had higher graduation and college enrollment (no size). Schoolwide study: graduation 85.7 percent before versus 83.2 percent in year 3 (not significant).
pathways.caveats: The schoolwide study has no comparison group. Prior-achievement controls in the matched study are unverified.

pathways.summary: A meta-analysis of Gaining Early Awareness and Readiness for Undergraduate Programs reports higher graduation and college enrollment, but the designs are unverified.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Effects range from small (college entrance test) to large (attendance); graduation and college enrollment higher for participants (no sizes).
pathways.caveats: The abstract does not say high school graduation, and pooled proportions may not compare with a control group.

pathways.summary: Programs for young people who have already left school raise completion of a high school equivalency credential, which does not count in the four-year graduation rate.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. These programs serve young people who have left school, so they do not touch the cohort graduation or dropout counts.
pathways.typicalEffect: YouthBuild: diploma or equivalency 54.6 versus 45.7 percent, all of it equivalency credentials (diploma 20.1 versus 22.1 percent); occupational license or certificate 4.1 versus 2.1 percent. National Guard Youth ChalleNGe: diploma or equivalency 60.5 versus 36.4 percent, mostly equivalency, with a smaller diploma gain (22.0 versus 16.3 percent). JOBSTART: 42 versus 28.6 percent, mostly equivalency.
pathways.caveats: The industry-credential base rate is under 5 percent and self-reported.

pathways.summary: A first-grade classroom package that included the Good Behavior Game raised graduation in one randomized cohort in Baltimore.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. The tested model was a teacher-delivered first-grade package (curriculum changes plus the game), not something a partner runs alone.
pathways.typicalEffect: Classroom-centered arm: adjusted graduation 61.9 versus 51.3 percent (odds ratio 1.70), larger for girls. Family-school partnership arm: 57.3 percent, no significant effect.
pathways.caveats: One cohort from the 1990s; graduation from district records plus equivalency.

pathways.summary: A kindergarten-age prevention program for disruptive boys in Montreal reduced dropout only indirectly, through less grade retention.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Indirect effect on dropout through fewer grade retentions and special-class placements; no direct effect reported; no size available.
pathways.caveats: One trial in Canada, checked from the abstract only.

pathways.summary: A family-strengthening program for Mexican American middle schoolers (Bridges to High School) lowered dropout indirectly, through school engagement.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Clearinghouse: did not drop out 88 versus 75 percent (420 students, significant). The authors report the effect as indirect (through engagement).
pathways.caveats: Dropout was mostly self- or parent-reported, with school records for 59 percent. One trial.

pathways.summary: A district course for Black male students in Oakland, taught by Black male teachers, went with fewer dropouts.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. A district course, not a partner program.
pathways.typicalEffect: Access to the African American Male Achievement initiative reduced Black male dropouts by 43 percent (5.2 to 3.0 per cohort of about 61) and raised one-year persistence about 3.6 points, mostly in ninth grade.
pathways.caveats: Based on state school-by-grade counts, not student records; one district.

pathways.summary: Tennessee's integrated student supports in schools did not change dropout.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No change in dropout or grade progression; small English gains and lower suspensions; chronic absence rose.
pathways.caveats: The rise in chronic absence matters for any attendance claim by community-schools partners.

pathways.summary: Online credit recovery for failed Algebra I led to fewer students recovering the credit than face-to-face classes, with no difference in graduation.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Chicago randomized trial: credit recovered 66 percent online versus 78 percent face to face; no significant later differences, including graduation. Expanding summer credit recovery raised recovery from 12 to 20 percent, with no detectable gain on tenth-grade tests.
pathways.caveats: Graduation effects are imprecise. Summer expansion results are preliminary.

pathways.summary: Positive family processes and parent involvement go with less absence and dropout, but the evidence does not show adjustment for prior achievement.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Meta-analysis: positive family processes related to less absence and dropout (strongest in primary school); no pooled size in the abstract. A national study: parent involvement explained truancy and dropout but not test scores.
pathways.caveats: Both checked from abstracts only.

pathways.summary: Pathways to Education, a neighborhood program of tutoring, mentoring, family support and financial aid, raised five-year graduation in Toronto.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Regent Park: five-year graduation up 15.2 points (38.2 to 53.4 percent); two later sites up 9.7 points.
pathways.caveats: One program in Canada, difference-in-differences design; five-year graduation.

pathways.summary: Achievement for Latinos through Academic Success, an attendance and family-contact program, cut ninth-grade dropout, but the gain faded by grade 11.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: End of grade 9: dropout 2 versus 17 percent; end of grade 11: enrolled 75 versus 66.7 percent, not significant.
pathways.caveats: Small 1990s trial in Los Angeles; the effect faded.

pathways.summary: Federally funded outside tutoring offered to students in low-performing schools (supplemental educational services) mostly did not raise state test scores.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Minneapolis: no significant differences. Los Angeles: not significant on state English or math. Jefferson County, Kentucky: small positive effects, not significant.
pathways.caveats: One New Jersey study claimed as null was found by the checker to show significant positive effects, so the record is mixed, not uniformly null.

pathways.summary: Giving children in high-poverty elementary schools free books they choose, repeatedly over several years, raises state reading test scores a little.
pathways.programModel: Free, child-selected books given every year for at least three years (about a dozen a year, for example at the end of each school year or in fall and spring), to children in high-poverty elementary schools. A single summer's book mailing does not qualify (see the row from PR-07).
pathways.typicalEffect: Randomized trial, 17 high-poverty schools (852 treatment, 478 control): 0.14 standard deviations on the state reading test after three summers, 0.21 for the most disadvantaged. Milwaukee school-level randomized trial (60 schools, Bernie's Book Bank): about 0.10 on the Wisconsin state reading test after five years.
pathways.caveats: The first trial was checked from its abstract only. The Milwaukee trial is a conference abstract with 59 percent attrition (differential under 1 point). One-summer book programs have null results at scale. Low cost.

pathways.summary: Mailing books to children for one summer did not raise reading scores at scale; it helped only when teachers and parents added reading support.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Books matched to reading level plus postcards: 0.02 standard deviations, not significant. A summer book program across schools: no overall effect, small gains in high-poverty schools and losses in moderate-poverty schools. Gains only for third-grade girls in another trial. Books with oral reading and comprehension support beat controls.

pathways.summary: Electronic books and independent silent reading programs did not improve reading comprehension.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Electronic books meta-analysis: overall 0.08, comprehension minus 0.014. Silent reading review: no meaningful benefit.
pathways.caveats: Too few high-quality studies.

pathways.summary: Competitive policy debate leagues for high school students went with higher English scores and graduation in Boston and Chicago.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Closest to qualifying; revisit if a second strong study appears.
pathways.typicalEffect: Boston: English test plus 0.13 standard deviations (student fixed effects); five-year graduation up 12 points (9 with a narrower comparison; the authors' conservative estimate is lower). Chicago: debaters 3.1 times more likely to graduate (association).
pathways.caveats: Only one strong quasi-experiment; the Chicago studies are associational with controls unconfirmed.

pathways.summary: Daily high-dosage tutorials in one Boston charter school raised grade 10 English scores.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: English plus 0.15 to 0.25 standard deviations a year; no average math gain. Meta-analysis of targeted school interventions: 0.22 short run, 0.05 at follow-up.
pathways.caveats: One school; a school-day structure.

pathways.summary: Intensive youth orchestra programs went with higher test scores for students who stayed, but students opt in.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Baltimore: long-term participants more often proficient in English (65.6 versus 30.8 percent on the older test). Los Angeles: English plus 26 points, math plus 17.
pathways.caveats: Groups were not fully equivalent after matching.

pathways.summary: A program of out-of-school learning activities with credit toward recognition (Children's University) gave small reading and math gains in England.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: About two months more progress in reading and math.
pathways.caveats: Low to moderate security; one trial outside the United States.

pathways.summary: City Year schools were more likely to raise proficiency rates in a study the program commissioned.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Partner schools 2 to 3 times more likely to raise English and math proficiency rates; about one month added learning.
pathways.caveats: School-level, commissioned by the program.

pathways.summary: A library literacy program has no test or school-record outcomes.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: No outcome measured.

pathways.summary: A summer family reading program showed larger reading growth in a sponsor-commissioned matched study.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Larger reading growth than matched students in several grades.
pathways.caveats: Selected high-fidelity districts; the often-quoted 0.33 comes from a secondary source.

pathways.summary: Text messages to parents of preschool and kindergarten children improved early literacy, with no follow-up to grade 3.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Preschool: early literacy about 0.11. Kindergarten: personalized texts beat general texts.
pathways.caveats: No grade 3 test.

pathways.summary: Cross-age peer tutoring helps both tutors and tutees in a meta-analysis of mixed designs.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Overall 0.34 (tutees 0.33, tutors 0.39).
pathways.caveats: Share of standardized measures unknown.

pathways.summary: An intensive summer algebra-readiness program raised end-of-summer math scores.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Elevate Math: 0.68 on a summer test.
pathways.caveats: No later state test or course outcome.

pathways.summary: A basketball-themed math program at a summer camp raised scores on a researcher test.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: 0.19 on a test built from national assessment items; under 20 dollars per student.
pathways.caveats: Not the state test; summer camp setting.

pathways.summary: Paying students for test results did not raise scores; paying for reading books raised reading in one city.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: New York and Chicago: no effect. Dallas reading: 0.18 to 0.25. Washington: reading marginal.

pathways.summary: City Connects, a school-based coordinator who reviews every student's strengths and needs and links them to services, went with higher grade 5 scores in a lottery-based study, but the gains did not survive correction for multiple tests.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Grade 5 (lottery-based comparison): math 0.21 and English 0.23 standard deviations, nominally significant, not significant after correction; estimates for students who took part were 0.57 and 0.63. A later study: nearly half a standard deviation in both subjects after five years. An earlier Boston study: higher report card and middle school scores.
pathways.caveats: All three studies come from the developer's research team. The two quasi-experiments' designs and sizes were partly unconfirmed.

pathways.summary: Family math activities at home did not raise children's math test scores in randomized trials.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Bedtime math app: not significant in the clearinghouse review (the authors report gains for children of math-anxious parents). Summer math at home with or without laptops: no difference on later achievement. Teachers Involve Parents in Schoolwork homework: higher scores in a quasi-experiment (test and size unconfirmed).
pathways.caveats: The only positive study is a quasi-experiment with unconfirmed details.

pathways.summary: Growth mindset and identity-affirming writing exercises did not raise math test scores reliably.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Growth mindset meta-analysis: 0.05, not significant after correcting for publication bias; 0.02 in the highest-quality studies. A Texas high school program: Algebra I end-of-course exam not significant. A values-affirmation replication near Philadelphia did not reproduce large earlier gains.

pathways.summary: Teaching math through career and technical courses (the Math-in-Career and Technical Education model) raised math scores in one randomized trial; a later study found no math gain.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Randomized trial: significantly better on two math tests, with no loss of technical skills. Later quasi-experiment: reading significant, math not.
pathways.caveats: Neither study used the Keystone Algebra I exam; it is a teacher model.

pathways.summary: Middle school partnerships with science museums (Urban Advantage in New York City) raised grade 8 science scores slightly.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. Revisit if an independent study replicates the result.
pathways.typicalEffect: At least 0.04 (about 0.05 to 0.06) standard deviations on the grade 8 science exam; some evidence of more passing a high school science exam; no effect on English or math. Larger for Hispanic and low-income students.
pathways.caveats: All three studies come from one research team using the same data, so they are one quasi-experiment, not independent replications.

pathways.summary: Out-of-school science, technology, engineering and math programs gave inconsistent science and math gains and did not raise attendance.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Tennessee summer camp: science 0.11 in the program year, minus 0.10 the next year; attendance not significant. Tennessee girls and boys program: one-year math 0.40 and science 0.32, two-year math 0.19. New York City design program randomized trial: no effect on any outcome. Massachusetts expanded learning time: generally no achievement effects, grade 5 science up in year 4; rated ineffective on tests. Baltimore program: math not significant, attendance 96.4 versus 95.6 percent.
pathways.caveats: Grantee studies with moderate baseline differences; the one randomized trial was null.

pathways.summary: School gardens and outdoor environmental education gave small or uncertain science gains.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: Garden program: higher but not significant in a multilevel model. National garden trial: very modest gains, scores poor in both groups. Pennsylvania outdoor watershed program: a significant difference on the state science test, with prior achievement possibly not adjusted.

pathways.summary: Text messages prompting parents to talk about science did not raise science scores.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit.
pathways.typicalEffect: England randomized trial (3,483 students): more science conversations, no detectable test effect, and less of other parent engagement.

pathways.summary: No rigorous United States study has tested a staff-support program a partner could run on teacher attendance.
pathways.programModel: Not used for credit. A gap.
pathways.typicalEffect: New York City mentoring of new teachers: weak evidence on absences. A teacher mindfulness program: better emotion regulation and classroom support, with no attendance outcome.

A-001.correct_citation: Lee, V. E., & Burkam, D. T. (2001). Dropping out of high school: The role of school organization and structure. Paper presented at the Harvard Civil Rights Project conference, January 13, 2001 (ERIC ED458694). Published version: American Educational Research Journal, 40(2), 353-393 (2003), doi:10.3102/00028312040002353.
A-001.design: Longitudinal, two-level HLM (NELS:88 High School Effectiveness Supplement, grade 10 in 1990 to grade 12 in 1992); adjusts for student background, grade 10 math achievement and grade 9-10 math GPA, and school average grade 8 math and grade 9 GPA
A-001.population_location: 3,840 students in 190 public, Catholic and independent high schools in the 30 largest US metropolitan areas
A-001.effect_as_reported: Coefficient -1.96 (1 SD better student-teacher relations = 86 percent lower odds of dropout) in small/medium public and Catholic schools; non-significant in independent schools (net .11) and large (.54) or very large (.69) schools
A-001.excerpt: In public or Catholic schools, of small or medium size, a 1 SD increase in positive student-teacher relations led to an 86 percent decrease in the odds of dropping out

A-002.correct_citation: Barile, J. P., Donohue, D. K., Anthony, E. R., Baker, A. M., Weaver, S. R., & Henrich, C. C. (2012). Teacher-student relationship climate and school outcomes: Implications for educational policy initiatives. Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 41(3), 256-267. doi:10.1007/s10964-011-9652-8
A-002.design: Longitudinal multilevel structural equation model (ELS:2002, sophomore 2002 to senior 2004); controls for sophomore math, school-level covariates and student background
A-002.population_location: 7,779 students in 431 US public high schools (national ELS:2002 sample)
A-002.outcome: Dropout by spring of senior year; gains in IRT math achievement
A-002.effect_as_reported: Positive TSR climate significantly and negatively related to log odds of dropout; no significant association with math achievement gains (coefficients not extracted)
A-002.excerpt: After controlling for sophomore-year math grades, school-level covariates, and student-level effects, a positive TSR climate during their sophomore year was found to be significantly and negatively related to the average log odds of student dropout

A-005.correct_citation: Gubbels, J., van der Put, C. E., & Assink, M. (2019). Risk factors for school absenteeism and dropout: A meta-analytic review. Journal of Youth and Adolescence, 48(9), 1637-1667.
A-005.design: Meta-analysis (three-level) of bivariate associations from longitudinal and cross-sectional studies; no adjustment for covariates; authors say causality cannot be concluded
A-005.population_location: Primary and secondary school students in Western countries (Europe, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, US)
A-005.effect_as_reported: Poor pupil-teacher relationship: absenteeism r = .294 (6 studies, 9 ES; .286 after trim-and-fill), p < .001; dropout r = .128 (4 studies, 10 ES), 95% CI -.013 to .269, p = .071 (trend)
A-005.excerpt: studies had to report on (1) a measure of bivariate association between a factor and school absenteeism or dropout (e.g., a correlation coefficient) or (2) sufficient information for calculating such an association

ATT-G044.correct_citation: Borman, G. D., Borman, T. H., Park, S. J., & Zhu, B. (2025). Replicating a middle-school belonging intervention: Evidence from a randomized trial within a new school district. AERA Open
ATT-G044.outcome: GPA, D/F grades, suspensions, referrals, attendance rate
ATT-G044.effect_as_reported: No significant main effects on academic or behavioral outcomes
ATT-G044.excerpt: we found no statistically significant main effects of treatment on any academic or behavioral outcomes.

B-002.correct_citation: Wu, H., Guo, Y., Yang, Y., Zhao, L., & Guo, C. (2021). A meta-analysis of the longitudinal relationship between academic self-concept and academic achievement. Educational Psychology Review, 33(4), 1749-1778.
B-002.design: Meta-analysis of 68 longitudinal studies (240 effect sizes); cross-lagged paths controlling for initial level of the outcome (prior achievement / prior self-concept)
B-002.population_location: Students across 68 longitudinal studies; location not stated in abstract
B-002.effect_as_reported: Achievement -> later ASC beta = 0.16; ASC -> later achievement beta = 0.08 (both p < .01); moderated by age, achievement level, measure type
B-002.excerpt: achievement significantly predicted ASC ([beta] = 0.16, p < 0.01) and vice-versa ([beta] = 0.08, p < 0.01) after controlling for the initial level of outcome variables

B-003.correct_citation: Marsh, H. W., Pekrun, R., & Lüdtke, O. (2022). Directional ordering of self-concept, school grades, and standardized tests over five years: New tripartite models juxtaposing within- and between-person perspectives. Educational Psychology Review, 34(4), 2697-2744. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09662-9
B-003.design: Longitudinal panel, five waves; CLPM and RI-CLPM cross-lagged models (autoregressive, so prior achievement controlled); covariates gender and primary-school math and verbal achievement
B-003.population_location: N = 3,425 students over five years of compulsory secondary schooling (country not stated in abstract)
B-003.outcome: Math self-concept, school grades, standardized achievement tests
B-003.effect_as_reported: Consistent support for reciprocal (bidirectional) effects across CLPM and RI-CLPM; no coefficients in abstract
B-003.excerpt: lag-2 paths between non-adjacent waves; and covariates (gender, primary-school math and verbal achievement). Across all basic and extended RI-CLPMs and CLPMs, there was consistent support for the REM bidirectional-ordering hypothesis

B-004.correct_citation: Talsma, K., Schüz, B., Schwarzer, R., & Norris, K. (2018). I believe, therefore I achieve (and vice versa): A meta-analytic cross-lagged panel analysis of self-efficacy and academic performance. Learning and Individual Differences, 61, 136-150. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2017.11.015
B-004.design: Systematic review and meta-analytic cross-lagged path analysis of two-wave longitudinal studies (pooled correlations; autoregressive paths control prior level)
B-004.population_location: k = 11 studies, N = 2,688; children and adults; location not stated
B-004.effect_as_reported: Performance -> later self-efficacy beta = 0.205; self-efficacy -> later performance beta = 0.071 (both p < .001); reciprocity for adults, not children
B-004.excerpt: Performance had a net positive effect on subsequent self-efficacy (β = 0.205, p < 0.001), significantly larger than the effect of self-efficacy on performance (β = 0.071, p < 0.001).

B-005.correct_citation: Sorjonen, K., Ingre, M., Melin, B., & Nilsonne, G. (2024). Questioning the reciprocal effects model of academic self-concept and achievement: A reanalysis of a meta-analysis of longitudinal studies and a simulation. SAGE Open, 14(4). https://doi.org/10.1177/21582440241292826
B-005.design: Methodological reanalysis of a published meta-analysis plus simulation; no new data
B-005.population_location: Not applicable (reanalysis of meta-analytic estimates; simulated data)
B-005.outcome: Academic self-concept and achievement (methodological critique of baseline-adjusted prospective effects)
B-005.effect_as_reported: Different plausible models support opposing claims; true prospective effects not necessary for observed meta-analytic associations
B-005.excerpt: prospective effects were estimated while adjusting for a prior measurement of the outcome, and this method is susceptible to spurious findings due to correlations with residuals and regression to the mean

B-008.correct_citation: Duncan, G. J., Dowsett, C. J., Claessens, A., Magnuson, K., Huston, A. C., Klebanov, P., Pagani, L. S., Feinstein, L., Engel, M., Brooks-Gunn, J., Sexton, H., Duckworth, K., & Japel, C. (2007). School readiness and later achievement. Developmental Psychology, 43(6), 1428-1446. https://doi.org/10.1037/0012-1649.43.6.1428
B-008.design: Secondary analysis of 6 longitudinal datasets with meta-analysis of coefficients; regressions with school-entry academic, attention and socioemotional skills entered together, most models controlling pre-school-entry cognitive, attention, socioemotional skills and family background
B-008.population_location: Six longitudinal datasets (US, UK, Canada per author list; countries not listed in abstract)
B-008.outcome: Later school reading and math achievement
B-008.effect_as_reported: School-entry math strongest, then reading, then attention; socioemotional behaviors generally insignificant; no coefficients in abstract
B-008.excerpt: By contrast, measures of socioemotional behaviors, including internalizing and externalizing problems and social skills, were generally insignificant predictors of later academic performance

B-010.correct_citation: Romano, E., Babchishin, L., Pagani, L. S., & Kohen, D. (2010). School readiness and later achievement: Replication and extension using a nationwide Canadian survey. Developmental Psychology, 46(5), 995-1007. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018880
B-010.design: Longitudinal survey secondary analysis (replication of Duncan et al. 2007 regression strategy); kindergarten predictors entered together
B-010.population_location: 1,521 children, National Longitudinal Survey of Children and Youth (NLSCY), Canada-wide; Study 2 adds Montreal (MLEPS)
B-010.outcome: Grade 3 math and reading (Study 1); grade 3 socioemotional outcomes (Study 2)
B-010.effect_as_reported: Math strongest predictor; literacy and mother-reported attention predicted later achievement; no coefficients in abstract
B-010.excerpt: (a) math skills were the strongest predictor of later achievement, (b) literacy and attention skills predicted later achievement, and (c) socioemotional behaviors did not significantly predict later school achievement.

B-012.correct_citation: Pagani, L. S., Fitzpatrick, C., Archambault, I., & Janosz, M. (2010). School readiness and later achievement: A French Canadian replication and extension. Developmental Psychology, 46(5), 984-994. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0018881
B-012.design: Prospective longitudinal population-based cohort, regression replicating Duncan et al. 2007; extension adds motor skills and classroom engagement
B-012.population_location: Population-based sample of French-speaking children in Quebec, Canada; MLEPS as reference group (N not in abstract)
B-012.outcome: End-of-grade-2 math, reading and general achievement; classroom engagement
B-012.effect_as_reported: Kindergarten math coefficients largest, then attention skills, receptive language, attention problems, behavior; no numbers in abstract
B-012.excerpt: In the replication model, kindergarten cognitive and attention characteristics predicted achievement by the end of 2nd grade.

B-013.correct_citation: McClelland, M. M., Acock, A. C., Piccinin, A., Rhea, S. A., & Stallings, M. C. (2013). Relations between preschool attention span-persistence and age 25 educational outcomes. Early Childhood Research Quarterly, 28(2), 314-324. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2012.07.008
B-013.design: Longitudinal cohort; structural equation modeling controlling for age-7 achievement (prior achievement), adopted status, vocabulary, gender, maternal education; logistic regression for college completion
B-013.population_location: N = 430 adopted and non-adopted children, Colorado Adoption Project (Colorado, US)
B-013.outcome: Math and reading achievement at age 21; college completion by age 25
B-013.effect_as_reported: 1 SD higher age-4 attention span-persistence = 48.7% greater odds of completing college by 25
B-013.excerpt: children's age 4 attention span-persistence significantly predicted math and reading achievement at age 21 after controlling for achievement levels at age 7, adopted status, child vocabulary skills, gender, and maternal education level

B-014.correct_citation: Morgan, P. L., Farkas, G., Hillemeier, M. M., Pun, W. H., & Maczuga, S. (2019). Kindergarten children's executive functions predict their second-grade academic achievement and behavior. Child Development, 90(5), 1802-1816.
B-014.design: Longitudinal, nationally representative, multi-year autoregressive panel with domain-specific and domain-general autoregressors (prior achievement and behavior controlled)
B-014.outcome: Grade 2 reading, mathematics, science achievement; behavioral self-regulation; problem behaviors
B-014.effect_as_reported: Working memory effects .08 SD (science) to .12 SD (mathematics); some effects about .04 SD
B-014.excerpt: working memory's predictive relations with children's academic achievement ranged from .08 of a standard deviation for science achievement to .12 of a standard deviation for mathematics achievement

B-015.correct_citation: Duckworth, A. L., Quinn, P. D., & Tsukayama, E. (2012). What No Child Left Behind leaves behind: The roles of IQ and self-control in predicting standardized achievement test scores and report card grades. Journal of Educational Psychology, 104(2), 439-451.
B-015.design: Two prospective longitudinal studies; SEM controlling for prior test scores and prior grades plus demographics (plus a third teacher-survey study)
B-015.population_location: Study 1: NICHD SECCYD children from 10 US sites (grade 4 predictors, grades 8-9 outcomes); Study 2: N = 510 middle school students in two schools
B-015.outcome: Change in standardized achievement test scores and report card grades / GPA
B-015.effect_as_reported: Study 1: test-score change self-control beta = .01 (p = .88), grades beta = .20; Study 2: tests beta = -.05 (p = .43), GPA beta = .22 (p < .001)
B-015.excerpt: IQ (β = .12, p < .001) but not self-control (β = −.05, p = .43) predicted standardized achievement test scores when controlling for prior-year standardized achievement test scores.

C-001.correct_citation: Aucejo, E. M., & Romano, T. F. (2014). Assessing the effect of school days and absences on test score performance. CEP Discussion Paper No. 1302, Centre for Economic Performance, LSE (September 2014). Published version: Economics of Education Review 55 (2016), 70-87.
C-001.design: Longitudinal administrative panel with student, teacher and school fixed effects (triple FE preferred spec); robustness with lagged test scores, family-year FE and flu-data IV for absences
C-001.population_location: North Carolina public school students, grades 3-5, 2006-2010 (NCERDC; about 1,000,903 student-year observations)
C-001.outcome: Standardized end-of-grade math and reading test scores
C-001.effect_as_reported: Table 11: absences x grade 3 = -0.0025 (math), -0.0015 (reading); grade 4 = -0.0054/-0.0030; grade 5 = -0.0088/-0.0042 SD per absence
C-001.excerpt: While each additional absence decreases math (reading) scores by 0.25% (0.15%) of a standard deviation in grade 3, by grade 5 each absences has about three times the impact.

C-002.correct_citation: Aucejo, E. M., & Romano, T. F. (2016). Assessing the effect of school days and absences on test score performance. Economics of Education Review, 55, 70-87.
C-002.design: Longitudinal administrative panel with fixed effects; robustness checks include flu-data instrument for absences, family-year fixed effects, excused vs unexcused absences, control for disengagement
C-002.population_location: North Carolina public school students (administrative data)
C-002.outcome: Standardized math and reading test scores
C-002.effect_as_reported: 10-day reduction in absences: +5.5 (math) and +2.9 (reading) percent of an SD; 10 extra school days: +1.7 and +0.8
C-002.excerpt: A similar reduction in absences would lead to gains of 5.5 in math and 2.9 in reading. We perform a number of robustness checks including utilizing flu data to instrument for absences, family-year fixed effects

C-003.correct_citation: Gottfried, M. A. (2009). Excused versus unexcused: How student absences in elementary school affect academic achievement. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 31(4).
C-003.design: Longitudinal multilevel administrative data; fixed effects model with classroom-level clustering
